In a first-of-its-kind experiment, physicists used pairs of entangled photons to verify a person's location. That's a step toward anchoring digital security to the physical world.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For the first time, physicists have used quantum entanglement to verify a person's physical location. That could one day make it much harder for hackers to pretend to be somewhere they're not, the team says.

In the new study, published Wednesday (Nov. 18) in the journal Nature, researchers at the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) used pairs of entangled photons (particles of light) to confirm that a participant was at a specific spot between two stations on NIST's campus in Boulder, Colorado. The method is called quantum position verification, and this is the first complete demonstration of it.

If the technology matures, it could help protect health records, stop remote attackers from sending commands to power grids or water treatment plants, block unauthorized stock trades and thwart phishing attacks carried out over phone or video calls, according to a statement.

"It's a totally new application for quantum networks," Shalm said. "You can add another layer of security to these systems that anchors a lot of this digital security to a position."

Location is a basic layer of security. Banks, power grids and government agencies often limit access to sensitive systems to people who are physically inside a secure building. But classical (nonquantum) ways of proving location remotely, which time how long signals take to travel, can be spoofed by hackers working together. Quantum physics can close that security gap, because a single quantum particle can't be copied.

"Is this call coming from my bank, or is it coming from someone in North Korea or somewhere else?" Krister Shalm, a quantum physicist at NIST who led the team, told Live Science. "That's really powerful if you can anchor digital security to a physical location."

In the experiment, the team used a technique called ranging, which is similar to the principles behind echolocation, radar and the lidar sensors found in some smartphones. It sends a signal and measures how long it takes for the response to return.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"You can send a signal at the speed of light and measure how long it takes to get back," Shalm told Live Science. "But the problem is, that's the thing that can always be spoofed classically."

In the experiment, two trusted stations called "verifiers" sat 640 feet (195 meters) apart, linked by cables and optical fibers running through the hallways of a NIST research building. A "prover," whose location the verifiers wanted to confirm, sat in between.

One verifier created pairs of entangled photons — particles so deeply linked that measuring one reveals something about the other, even when they're separated at great distances. The verifier kept one photon from each pair and sent its twin to the prover. At the same time, both verifiers sent random bits of information that were timed to reach the prover at the same moment.

The prover combined the two inputs with a simple math operation and used the result to decide how to measure the photon's polarization ‪—‬ the direction in which its electric field oscillates. The measuring device works much like the filter in polarized sunglasses. A detector then recorded whether the photon made it through the filter, and the prover sent that yes-or-no result back to both verifiers.

Because nothing travels faster than light, the round-trip time told the verifiers how far away the prover could be. And because the photon can't be copied, the measurement had to be made in that exact spot.

To confirm that no one cheated, the team ran a loophole-free Bell test, which checks whether particles are more strongly correlated than classical physics allows. If anyone tampers with the photons or the equipment, the test fails. Shalm led one of the first such tests in 2015.

NIST physicist Krister Shalm performing a Bell test in 2015. Shalm was part of the team that demonstrated the new location verification method.

Scientists first proposed position verification in the late 2000s, but the experiments are extremely demanding, Shalm said. Many earlier designs could tolerate losing only a few percent of the photons along the way, which is "just not practical or reasonable" with today's technology. The NIST team relied on superconducting detectors that catch nearly every photon.

The surprise, Shalm said, was that the Bell test approach worked at all on the first try. It offers the strongest security of any quantum protocol because it makes very few assumptions about how the equipment works, but it is usually the hardest to pull off. "The sort of gold-plated deluxe version — you were able to do that on the first demonstration of a full protocol," he said.

The system ran about 250,000 trials per second. Each verification required 30 million to 60 million rounds of signals sent back and forth ‪—‬ roughly two to four minutes of data. Over two days in fall 2024, the team ran 335 verifications, and nearly all of them passed. The prover's location was confirmed within a region about 4.5 times smaller in volume than what a comparable classical method could guarantee, the team said.

The experiment proved secure against attackers who shared little or no entanglement of their own. Protecting against attackers with more powerful quantum resources will require longer strings of random bits, the researchers wrote.

The initial users of this technology are expected to be data centers, financial backend systems and critical infrastructure like power plants, Shalm said. However, incorporating this technology into cellphones will take significantly longer, as the components are currently too large and expensive.

"In terms of a computer analogy, we are much closer to the building-sized computers of the 1950s and 1960s than today's smartphones," he said in an email. "However, with consistent improvement it might be possible in several decades to come up with a compact handheld version of the devices needed for quantum position verification."

Real-world use may be more than a decade away, Scott Glancy, a NIST physicist and study co-author, said in the statement. To verify that a customer is truly communicating with someone from their bank, high-quality quantum networks must be utilized to share entangled photons between the two parties.

The team already knows how to speed things up. Faster measurement devices could cut each verification from minutes to about a second, according to the study, and low-latency communication links could shrink the verified zone to a single building, even with stations miles apart.

"It may not be this year, but I think it's something that we're building towards, and we know the steps that are needed to get there," Shalm said.

Kavuri, G. A., Zhang, Y., Gookin, A. R., Patra, S., Bienfang, J. C., Fu, H., Alnawakhtha, Y., Reddy, D., V., Mazurek, M. D., Abellán, C., Amaya, W., Mitchell, M. W., Miller, C. A., Mirin, R. P., Stevens, M. J., Glancy, S., Knill, E., & Shalm, L. K. (2026). Quantum position verification with remote untrusted devices. Nature. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11247-3

#6357. Where is freshwater wildlife under the most pressure? A new map offers surprises

A global study maps 45 threats to 21,490 freshwater species and reveals where conservation plans based on land wildlife can miss areas of high risk.

Rivers, lakes and wetlands are home to nearly a third of all known vertebrate species.

A new global study maps where 45 human pressures, from crop farming to dam construction, are most likely to affect freshwater wildlife.

A team led from McGill University analyzed 21,490 species and found that freshwater threat hotspots often differ from those on land.

For the threats compared, freshwater mammals generally faced greater pressure than land mammals, with a smaller gap for reptiles.

Christophe Brabant, a doctoral student in biology at McGill University, led the work with biology professor Lars Lønsmann Iversen, a member of McGill’s Bieler School of Environment.

The researchers drew on expert assessments to identify the threats facing each species.

They combined those assessments with species’ known ranges to map where the threats are most likely to affect them.

The researchers identified three threats that were especially widespread.

Across river sub-basins worldwide, they estimated that each affected roughly one in four freshwater species present, on average. Farmland growing crops came first.

Dams and other water management came second, and runoff from farms and forestry third.

Europe and northwestern Africa’s Maghreb region carry the heaviest combined load of all 45 threats. In Europe, the dominant problem is pollution from cities, farms and industry.

In the Maghreb it is pollution plus dams and heavy water use. Other hot spots include the Nile, the Niger Delta and the Rift Valley lakes of East Africa.

The lightest loads are where few people live, in Siberia and northern Canada, and in the Sahara, Arabian and Australian deserts.

Global averages hide big differences between animals. Fish are mainly hit by fishing across 37% of their range and by dams across another 30.5%.

Farming was the leading threat across 45.8% of amphibians’ combined range and 31.45% of the combined range of dragonflies and damselflies.

The authors linked this pattern to the animals’ reliance on both land and water at different stages of life.

Freshwater reptiles and mammals face a different enemy. Hunting and other direct use are the main threat across 37.8% of reptile ranges and 43.4% of mammal ranges.

That covers the wildlife trade, traditional medicine, animals caught in fishing gear and animals killed on purpose.

In an interview with Earth.com, Brabant noted that dams, farmland, and farm pollution are widespread, but their weight changes from region to region and group to group.

“This means there is no one-size-fits-all approach to freshwater conservation,” he said.

The raw material was the Red List kept by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, which records for each assessed species the threats experts have seen affecting it.

The team took five groups that have been assessed in full: amphibians, fish, mammals, reptiles, and the dragonflies and damselflies.

For each species, they combined its range map with its threat list.

“By combining this data, we could calculate, for any sub-watershed, the probability that a species occurring there is affected by a particular threat,” Brabant said.

One map per threat per group made 225 maps, which the team stacked into a single index of combined pressure.

Species with small ranges were given more weight.

A threat recorded for a species found in one lake can be placed on the map with confidence, while one recorded for a species spread across a continent can’t.

To test whether the maps mean anything for survival, the team compared them with two separate records.

In the 5% of river basins where extinction risk is modeled to be highest, 71% of the 45 threats were more likely to affect a species than their global average.

The second record was the Living Planet Index, which tracks counts of individual animal populations over time.

Across 2,568 freshwater vertebrate populations from 600 species, populations were shrinking faster in basins with a heavier combined threat load.

Neither record was used to build the maps, so the match is not circular.

The authors wrote that it suggests the maps capture where threats are already pushing freshwater species toward decline.

The study also lined up the freshwater maps against earlier ones made the same way for land vertebrates.

For all seven threats that had been mapped on land, freshwater mammals were more likely to be affected than land mammals.

Freshwater reptiles showed the same pattern with a smaller gap, which the authors put down to the time reptiles still spend on land.

The hot spots were in different places, too. Where freshwater fish and frogs are under the most pressure is not where land vertebrates are.

“What surprised me most was how different the geography was,” Brabant told Earth.com. Conservation planning has often relied on information about land species, he said.

That is why freshwater species and their threats need to be written into plans explicitly if the plans are going to reach them.

The Red List treats each threat as if it acted alone, and the authors wrote that many of them combine in ways that could make the damage worse.

The maps estimate how likely species are to be affected in each area. They don’t measure how much harm each threat causes.

Range maps describe where species live today, so places a threat has already emptied may not show up.

Asked which places he would look at first, Brabant said threat alone isn’t enough. Europe and northwestern Africa lead on accumulated threats, while many tropical regions stand out for the number of species affected.

“Areas of high richness and high threat suggest that threat mitigation is most urgent, whereas areas of high richness and low threats would be most suitable for proactive protection,” he said.

What would help most right now, he said, is reducing the pressures: cleaner water, protected habitat and rivers reconnected. But the most useful action depends on the place and the species.

The next step is matching each basin’s threats to the conservation actions that address them, which the maps alone can’t do yet.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

#6356. The Book Lover’s Gift Guide

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Science News staff loved books about dinosaurs, parenting and numbers in 2026

Science News staff devoured books of all kinds this year, on topics ranging from ecology and evolution to the human brain and mathematics. We covered it all — even a cookbook! These 10 titles rose to the top of our 2026 reading list and could make great gifts for the book lovers in your life. —  Anna Mattson, Assistant Editor

Big thinkers will love Huge Numbers, a fascinating look into the study of large numbers. “When I think of big numbers, I usually think of a 1 with a lot of zeroes tacked on the end. But the reality is much more complex than I ever imagined,” says senior physics writer Emily Conover. The book, among Conover’s favorites of the year, “provided me with a new appreciation of our number system and the creative ways mathematicians have expanded it to express ever-larger numbers,” she says. “Plus, contemplating unfathomably large figures makes my own concerns seem insignificant.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Staff writer Erin Garcia de Jesús’ favorite book of 2026, The Creatures’ Guide to Caring, will strike a chord with new parents. “Between sleepless nights and poopy diapers, there’s not much to laugh about in the early days of parenting. But I found plenty of humor (and plenty to be grossed out about) in The Creatures’ Guide to Caring,” Garcia de Jesús says. “It’s the perfect book to make anyone, parent or otherwise, feel better that we’re not the only animals struggling with our offspring.”

Merritt R. TuretskyW.W. Norton & Company | $29.99

Adventure seekers will lose themselves in the mesmerizing ecosystems at the heart of Bogland, biomedical sciences writer Aimee Cunningham’s favorite book of the year. Ecologist Merritt R. Turetsky immerses readers in these waterlogged landscapes that are often overlooked and underestimated. “I am firmly on team boglands after reading about the beauty and wonder of these ecosystems,” Cunningham says.

Senior writer Meghan Rosen’s favorite book of 2026 is perfect for anyone interested in — or wary of — health and wellness culture. Morbid exposes the lack of science behind a lot of antiaging advice, such as eating like centenarians do and taking “anti­aging” supplements. “Turns out, a lot of it is just plain bunk,” Rosen says. “Skeptical readers will enjoy Newman’s takedowns, which go down smoothly with a healthy dose of humor.”

Senior neuroscience writer Laura Sanders’ pick for 2026 is a must-read for any expecting mother, new mother or person looking to learn about how pregnancy and motherhood impact the body. “A Mother’s Brain reads like a scientific love letter to moms, who all too often get overlooked,” she says. Author and neuroscientist Susana Carmona “covers the nascent field of matrescence in lively, vivid chapters. And along the way, she convincingly argues that the maternal brain is compelling, wondrous and still mysterious,” Sanders says.

Those who listen to true crime podcasts or wish spooky season lasted all year long will enjoy Exhumed, an exploration of the lore and medical practices leading up to the 19th century New England vampire panic. “Thanks to Mahnke’s gripping prose, I felt like I was in the middle of the action. It was hard to lay the book down,” assistant editor Anna Mattson wrote in her online review. Mattson notes that Exhumed, her favorite read of 2026, is littered with bizarre facts that would be perfect for invigorating dull conversations.

For the anthropologist in your life, try The Story of Stories — a deep dive into how technological upheavals have shaped storytelling throughout history. The author provides what Sanders describes as scattershot history lessons in her online review: “Ashton has a knack for pulling out memorable bits from historical records, scientific studies and other sources for readers.”

Alexis Nikole NelsonSimon & Schuster | $35.00

Conover couldn’t pick just one favorite. For people who enjoy getting creative in the kitchen, she recommends Happy Snacking, Don’t Die! “This cookbook provides such a joyful how-to on foraging and eating wild plants,” Conover says. “It helped me see my plant neighbors in a whole new light. And I got to make some tasty treats to share with my family as well.”

Tyrant Lizard Queen is the only work of fiction on our list. But it’s rooted in real science, and stars a Tyrannosaurus rex. Author Riley Black “offers an empathetic look at a real-life creature that experienced hunger and pain, much like the animals that surround us today,” says Science News Explores assistant editor Aaron Tremper, who chose the book as his favorite of 2026. “Black’s penchant for story makes for a thrilling read that fans of Jurassic Park and King Kong can get behind.”

And for those interested in bioethics, we suggest picking up Every Living Creature. Author and physician Joshua D. Mezrich offers a comprehensive look at the field of xenotransplantation, through the stories of courageous doctors and patients who helped make it possible. “At times, the story can feel like a whirlwind, whisking readers across decades and from lab to lab and surgery to surgery,” Rosen wrote in her online review. “But at its core, Every Living Creature is a book about hope.”

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

A version of this article appears in the November 21, 2026 issue of Science News.

Anna Mattson is the assistant editor at Science News. Her freelance work has been published in Grist, Scientific American, Inside Climate News and elsewhere, on topics ranging from wildfires in the West to Superfund contamination.

#6355. The 8 Best Solar Generators Provide Reliable Backup Power in a Pinch

These tested and researched models from Jackery, EcoFlow, Anker, and other trusted brands are the ones we stand behind and recommend.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Power stations (i.e., solar generators) have become increasingly popular because they are easy to run, cost less over time than gas generators, and offer eco-friendly, emission-free operation, especially when paired with a solar panel. Some are small and compact, ideal for off-grid adventures, while larger ones are able to back up critical home circuits during a blackout.

Unlike fuel-based generators, solar generators can’t create electricity in real time. They’re giant battery packs, not true generators, and need to be recharged using alternating current (AC) power or solar panels, the latter of which often takes many hours in ideally sunny conditions.

Despite those distinctions compared to portable generators, there’s nothing more convenient than a power station for charging or running everything you need for day-to-day life—phones and laptops, lights, and even a small appliance or two. Plus, it’s nice to have a device that doesn’t produce carbon emissions and replenishes itself freely from the sun’s rays. Whether you’re seeking a highly portable option or need one that’s heavy-duty enough for extended use, these are the best solar generators we’ve tested and researched to date.

To pick the best solar generators, we tested some of these power stations for charging capacity, ease of use, weight, and different use cases. Our picks were reviewed by Popular Mechanics editor Brad Ford, who provided input for the larger-capacity units. Other models on this list were reviewed by test editor David Dritsas or freelance writer Maggie Slepian.

Our primary concerns were portability and convenience. Ease of use was also important—was the display easy to read? Did the screen readouts make sense? Bonus points if we could tell how much power is available at a glance. In the past few years, these criteria have become easier to meet. There are now plenty of compact, affordable units that have better charging capabilities than before.

Very few power stations of this size can handle as much solar input power as the Bluetti Apex 200. With two input types—low-voltage XT60 (up to 1,000 watts) and high-voltage MC4 (up to 2,000 watts)—it can accept up to 3,000 watts of solar power. If you had the panels and ideal weather, you could fully charge this station in less than 2 hours—even faster than plugging it into the wall. That’s impressive.

It also balances nicely between being a portable station and a home backup solution. It offers 3,200 watts of continuous power (it says 3,600 on the front, but that’s only if it’s connected to an expansion battery). We were able to power a refrigerator for a full 27 hours on a single charge, and estimated the battery efficiency at 90 percent, which is very good. Meanwhile, the 2,560-watt-hour battery capacity is expandable by adding up to six additional batteries. Using Bluetti’s largest battery, the B500K, you could build a massive 33-kilowatt-hour system.

While 3,600 watts isn’t enough to power a whole home, you could power a couple of circuits through a manual transfer switch using the 120-volt 30-amp output. But keep in mind that there’s no 240-volt support, so you can’t use it to power high-voltage appliances like electric dryers.

As a portable station, the Apex 200 has a lot to offer. At 59 pounds, it’s not too hard to move around the house or in and out of a vehicle. And there are several great DC power options, including a bank of USB outlets (two are high-power USB-C) and both 10- and 30-amp, 12-volt outputs. We also love that the AC ports can individually be turned on and off using the mobile app; this helps improve overall runtime.

Since very few stations can match its max solar input capacity, we concluded that the Apex 200 is definitely a top choice for anyone who wants a power station that can recharge using the sun’s rays, but also offers the versatility of being used on the road or at home.

Full Bluetti Apex 200 Power Station Review

This model replaces the original Jackery 1000, but many of the same observations made of the first model still apply. The new version has a slightly higher capacity of 1,070 watt-hours and uses a newer lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) battery, which is a newer battery technology that offers a longer lifespan (4,000 cycles versus 500 cycles for this model) and better performance in extreme temperatures.

Expert Maggie Slepian used the previous model on a media trip where she had to keep multiple camera batteries charged during a weeklong outing. She found that while the capacity was lower than you'll find with others on this list, it actually powers items for longer than some higher-capacity models. She also charged her photographer’s camera batteries while charging the power bank on solar power (it was a very sunny winter day), which proved effective and efficient.

The newer V2 model has seven ports, including three AC outlets, two USB-C ports (one 30-watt and one 100-watt), a 12-volt car port, and one standard 18-watt USB-A outlet. It charges a typical laptop eight times or powers a small refrigerator or an electric cooler for over 15 hours.

The Jackery Explorer 1000 V2 charges with a 200-watt solar panel or a 12-volt outlet in your vehicle while you’re on the move. It has fairly standard charging times, with 11.5 hours in a car outlet, 6.5 hours for solar panels, and just 5.5 hours to fully charge in a wall outlet. This won’t be your best bet for powering larger appliances, but it’s an ideal power station for smaller items and off-grid camping.

The EcoFlow Delta Pro is a large portable power station with an output that rivals some gas portable generators. When sold in a bundle with solar panels, like the package with two 220-watt portable panels we tested, it becomes a powerful solar generator. With an output of 3,600 watts, the Delta Pro can charge multiple appliances, and the output has the ability to bump up to 4,500 watts with its built-in X-Boost technology if more power is needed.

To get an idea of the run time, we used the Delta Pro to power a full-size, 25-cubic-foot refrigerator—which it did for a remarkable 51 hours and 24 minutes. When recharged from a standard outlet, it took only two hours and 36 minutes. But it also charges with the included adapter, at electric vehicle charging stations, with a DC car adapter, or with the solar panels that come with the unit. Through the 30-amp connection, you can also connect this to a transfer switch to directly power select circuits in your home.

Like any power station with a large battery capacity, it will take a long time, perhaps nearly two days, to recharge this station using the bundled 220-watt solar panels. The good news is the Delta Pro accepts up to 1,600 watts of solar input, so it can charge faster by connecting more panels.

The heavy-duty wheels and telescoping handle on Anker’s Solix F3000 are easy to use, allow you to stand upright when pulling, and are a dream for people who regularly find themselves moving their power station around, whether it’s at a campsite or to different parts of the house during a power outage.

Along with convenience, this generator is a powerhouse with the capacity to easily run your refrigerator or a greenhouse heater, or keep your RV bright and warm.

We were impressed with Anker’s app, which allows us to check the charging status or power being generated without continually going outside to check. The app also lets you turn the power to the AC and USB ports on and off remotely, keeping tabs on how much energy is being utilized.

The Solix F3000 has 11 ports, including two car ports, an RV-specific outlet, four AC ports, three USB-C charging ports, and two USB-A. In sunny conditions and moderate temperatures, it recharges with a 400-watt solar panel in just a few hours and supports up to 2,400 watts of solar input.

One of Jackery’s most recent solar generators is also its most rugged, able to withstand the elements better than most. It achieves this with an IP65 weatherproof rating, molded rubber port covers, a shockproof enclosure, and a bottom drainage system, which is part of a titanium alloy cooling structure that helps keep water out of the enclosure.

We got a chance to see these features up close and were impressed by them all, as well as a very sturdy enclosure that, thanks to the cooling system design, eliminates any side vents that could allow water to get inside. It feels strong; you could bang this station around without worrying too much about damaging it. The only downside is that this denser construction adds a bit of weight.

As a power station, it delivers 1,800 watts of output with a battery capacity of 1,536 watt-hours. That’s enough power for a weekend camping trip or for running low-powered small appliances and some lighting during an emergency. As a solar generator, it can handle up to 800 watts of input from a portable panel. We paired it with a Jackery 200-watt panel, and it worked well. Overall, if your off-road adventures often get a little dirty, but you need some extra power, the Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra Power Station is a good one to have at your side.

Full Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra Power Station Review

The latest version of the Goal Zero Yeti 1500 is a well-designed power station that’s ideal for off-grid camping situations where dust, wind, and potentially wet conditions are always on the table. This 2,000-watt power station is weatherproof with an IPX4 rating and features outlet shields that cover the ports and inputs. Each section is well-lit by an LED light that’s individually turned on or off using a manual button or the mobile app (and will shut off if not used after a certain period).

There’s a healthy number of outputs on the Yeti 1500, including four 120-volt AC outlets, four (two are high-powered) USB-A ports, and four 12-volt connections. We simulated an emergency blackout and managed to run a cable modem with a WiFi router, a lamp, a TV, and a tower fan, while charging a phone and a laptop through the USB-C ports. Given the station’s output and capacity, there was enough power for over two days of use (conveniently shown on the main display), and there was plenty of room to spare for a few more devices.

To test its solar capabilities, we paired the Yeti 1500 with a Nomad 200-watt portable solar panel and connected it using the high-voltage DC input, which accepts up to 600 watts; however, it also features a low-voltage input that accepts up to 300 watts for smaller panel arrays. Because both inputs can be used simultaneously, you could theoretically pair with two arrays for up to 900 watts, which is a high amount of input for a station of this size.

Of course, no portable panel operates at 100 percent efficiency. Even on a sunny, cloudless day with no shade-causing obstructions, the input readings showed anywhere from 125 to 145 watts. After initiating a recharge with only 5 percent capacity left, it would take at least 10.5 hours in those conditions to recharge. That’s actually not bad. An average of about 70 percent efficiency for a portable panel is good.

This power station takes solar recharging seriously. The Elite 300 can accept up to 1,200 watts of input, which is a high amount for a station this size. We paired it with a 250-watt portable panel and, on a fully sunny day, got around 260 watts of input. That’s the typical efficiency of a portable panel (again, you’ll never get 100 percent). But pair it with some larger panels, and you’ll get even more.

It also boasts an impressive battery capacity of just over 3,000 watt-hours and 2,400 watts of output, which is high for a station of this size. Plus, it includes a 120-volt 30-amp port, which is handy for connecting it to a small RV or pop-up camper, allowing you to run small appliances and water pumps. It’s not enough power to run a heating or cooling system for a significant amount of time, but for lights, small appliances, and other items that need power, this station will deliver.

If there’s one downside we found, it’s that there’s no way to add an expansion battery to increase your capacity. That’s not a huge detractor, but it’s something we’ve seen in stations even smaller than this one. But at the end of the day, the Bluetti Elite 300 solar generator offers the right balance between a midsize power station that delivers a lot of power and run time, and a station that is compact and portable enough to be perfectly suited for an outdoor adventure.

Full Bluetti Elite 300 Solar Generator Review

The Anker Solix C2000 power station can deliver the full 2,400 watts of output to the bank of five AC outlets—something similar stations don’t offer. This allows you to power several things at once, like a refrigerator, toaster, router, and chargers, all at the same time.

During our tests, we were able to take full advantage of this, powering a refrigerator (by itself for up to 18 hours), along with some high-powered appliances, like a four-slot toaster and an electric kettle (though not the last two at the same time).

Another interesting ability of the C2000 is that you can fast charge it from AC power up to 1,800 watts, but that recharging rate remains consistent if you’re powering other devices at the same time (we confirmed this with a wattmeter). For example, we ran a 1,400-watt space heater while still recharging at the full 1,800-watt rate. Other power stations offer similar fast charging but will throttle the amount of power coming into the station while powering devices.

For solar recharging, we were a bit disappointed that this station can only accept 800 watts of input; other stations of this size accept more. But when solar was plugged in, it worked well. We connected it to a 200-watt Anker portable panel, and in full sun, we were getting around 125 to 145 watts of input, which is pretty good as these types of panels go. The C2000 is not IPX-rated for any type of weather resistance, however, so we would not recommend leaving this station sitting outside if the weather turns wet.

Full Anker Solix C2000 Power Station Review

Power stations use watts and watt-hours to express size and capacity. Watts (size) refer to how much power it produces. For example, if you need to run a 900-watt microwave, you’ll need a station that outputs at least that much power (ideally more, since factory specs are never exact).

Meanwhile, watt-hours (capacity) give you an idea of how long devices can be powered continuously, though how much time depends on the amount of power being drawn—watt-hours don’t dictate a set time frame. Higher-powered devices will drain the battery a lot faster than lower-powered ones.

That may seem confusing, but a simple equation gives you an approximate idea of how it works: total watt-hours (of the generator) ÷ watts (of the device) = hours the power station runs.

For example, if you had a power station with a 2,048-watt-hour capacity and wanted to run a 750-watt space heater consistently at its highest setting, it would probably run for around 2.5 hours, so long as nothing else is plugged in. But for a refrigerator, whose power draw fluctuates between 10 and 300 watts (depending on how often the compressor turns on), you might be able to run it for nearly 24 hours.

Keep in mind that manufacturer specs are taken from perfect conditions; in the real world, you’ll likely see slightly less capacity from your power station. If you’re not sure how much power the different devices in your home draw, sometimes it’s written on a label, or you can use a device like a wattmeter.

Just as a power station has specifications on output size and capacity, solar panels are rated by how many watts they produce for a device after they convert the sun’s rays into electrical current (e.g., 100 watts, 200 watts, etc.). Because real-world conditions are never perfect, it’s not uncommon for panels to only output 50 to 75 percent (or even lower) of their total potential.

Your panels must also be within the acceptable input range of the power station. For example, connecting a 400-watt solar-panel array to a power station that only accepts 110 watts of solar input can cause an overload and damage the station.

While weight and size don’t directly correlate to the technicalities of power banks, they impact the convenience of each model. Many camping and overlanding setups have limited space, so the more compact models likely have a higher appeal as a result.

That said, most units weigh at least 10 pounds, and the weight and size increase quickly with greater capacities. Before purchasing, consider where you plan to store the power bank and the space in your vehicle or camper where it will live while you’re on the road. If you plan to use this power bank solely as a home backup option, portability will matter less, but consider how much effort it will take to move it around within your home or in your outdoor space.

I am a low-maintenance camper, and most of my background is in lightweight backcountry travel. That means I prioritize space-saving and ease-of-use, so my go-to power banks have between 250 and 600 watt-hours, and weigh less than 15 pounds.

This is perfect for a weekend trip, with the on-the-go (car or solar) charging capabilities to put my mind at ease for longer trips. Mostly, I’m charging small items, so one charge lasts a long time. However, plenty of people in the van-life and remote-work world are powering their RVs and vans, and relying on multiple laptop charges. For that, I’d recommend one of the larger units.

A solar-powered generator charges and runs almost anything that requires power—it just depends on the capacity. These generators can charge power tools in the shop, laptops for remote work, and personal devices like Bluetooth headphones and speakers.

A solar-powered generator with a higher power capacity can even power household appliances in the event of a power outage. And the fact that these are solar-compatible means you aren’t reliant on the electrical grid to recharge them.

Every unit on our list has multiple charging options, including wall (AC outlet), car (12-volt), and solar. Each input method charges your unit at a different speed, and solar also depends on the conditions. AC power is the fastest, followed by 12-volt, and then by solar (though a larger solar array could potentially be faster than 12-volt).

I try to charge up my power banks whenever I can, so I’m never caught off guard trying to leave on a trip with a dying power bank. If this happens (which it has), I’ll charge it in my vehicle’s 12-volt port while I’m driving, though this is often slower than solar or a wall unit.

Solar power is the most sustainable and typically fastest way to power these—just be sure you have enough wattage in the solar panels to make it effective. I recommend keeping the generator stored with at least an 80 percent charge, and unplugging it once it’s fully charged—keeping it plugged in longer than necessary degrades the battery.

Most units will have a simple readout display showing the remaining battery charge, and it’s a good practice not to allow your battery pack to get below 20 percent.

David is a Reviews Editor for Hearst’s Enthusiast Group, contributing to Popular Mechanics, Runner’s World, Bicycling, Best Products, and Biography. He also spent years covering the ever-changing world of online retail. To relax, he loves experimenting with new recipes, tweaking his smart home setup, and spending time outdoors on his bike or camping.

#6354. Why does Webb see so many giant galaxies in the early universe?

The Lumina simulation traces how stars and quasars transformed gas in the early universe and explores why Webb sees so many massive galaxies.

The first stars and galaxies gave off ultraviolet light that stripped electrons from hydrogen atoms between galaxies.

Quasars later began stripping helium of its last electron, a process that took more energetic light and was still underway long after most of the hydrogen had been ionized.

A new computer simulation called Lumina tracks how gas, dark matter and light interacted through both changes.

It models a region that would span about 1.6 billion light-years on each side at today’s cosmic scale, giving astronomers a way to test their predictions against observations from the James Webb Space Telescope.

Oliver Zier, a fellow at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, led the project.

Aaron Smith of the University of Texas at Dallas was a co-author, along with colleagues at MIT, York University and the Max Planck Institute for Astrophysics.

“With JWST, the early universe has become an exciting new frontier in astrophysics,” Zier said. “To understand what we are seeing with this telescope, we need to translate our theories into detailed predictions.”

A simulation is that translation. Astronomers feed in the laws of physics and the universe’s starting conditions, then let a supercomputer calculate how everything develops over time.

They compare the result with real telescope images. A match gives astronomers more confidence in the model. A mismatch can show where its assumptions need more testing.

Lumina covers roughly the first 2 billion years, following the earliest galaxies and the thin gas between them.

The simulated cube is about 1.6 billion light-years on a side, more than 100 times the volume of comparable simulations.

The team divided its contents into 432 billion pieces of gas and dark matter, and each piece of gas has about 3.6 million times the mass of the Sun.

Galaxies grow where the dark matter gathers, strung along the filaments of the cosmic web.

The team ran Lumina on Frontier, a supercomputer at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee.

The simulation used 7,536 graphics accelerators, just over 20% of the machine, and about 600 terabytes of working memory at its peak.

Smith described what that size makes possible.

“For the first time, we can follow along as both hydrogen and helium changed into their modern form across such an enormous volume of the universe, while still resolving the galaxies and other luminous objects driving that transformation,” he said.

Earlier simulations of this kind, including the Thesan project, stopped before helium began to clear. Lumina’s cube is 144 times the volume of Thesan’s.

The first stars and galaxies cleared the hydrogen slowly and unevenly. In Lumina, bubbles of cleared gas open around the biggest galaxies first and grow until they merge. Regions far from any galaxy stay foggy longest.

The team divided the simulation into 125 regions and tracked how quickly the hydrogen changed in each one.

In a typical region, nearly all of the hydrogen gas between galaxies had lost its electrons by about 1.1 billion years after the Big Bang. In the slowest regions, that took about 1.3 billion years.

Astronomers see the same late finish in the light of distant quasars, which still shows absorption by hydrogen gas at that time.

Stars did nearly all of this work. Quasars supplied about 15% of the hydrogen-clearing light near the end.

Clearing helium takes light about four times more energetic than clearing hydrogen, and ordinary stars give off very little of it. Quasars do.

A quasar is a supermassive black hole pulling in gas so fast that the gas shines with intense ultraviolet light.

In Lumina, the brightest quasars began stripping helium of its last electron about 900 million years after the Big Bang. The process was about halfway complete by 1.5 billion years.

By 2 billion years, the regions where helium still held its last electron accounted for less than 1% of the space Lumina modeled.

The bubbles around quasars grew larger than the hydrogen bubbles that formed around galaxies.

Each clearing also heats the gas. The thin gas between galaxies warms to roughly 18,000°F to 36,000°F (10,000°C to 20,000°C) while the hydrogen clears.

It cools as the universe expands, then warms again when the quasar light reaches it.

Measurements of the helium clearing are scarce. Most studies of it rely on fewer than about 25 quasars with a usable line of sight, and Lumina’s timing agrees with those measurements.

Lumina also grows galaxies, and here it fails a test. At about 1.2 billion years after the Big Bang and earlier, the simulation produces fewer very massive galaxies than Webb has found.

The shortfall grows the further back in time the comparison goes.

The team wrote that this confirms a known problem: galaxy models tuned to the nearby universe undercount the giants Webb sees in the early one.

Stars might form more efficiently in the earliest big galaxies, or the masses astronomers read off Webb’s images might be less certain than assumed.

The simulation can’t settle that on its own, but it marks where the standard picture falls short.

Some of Lumina’s agreement with observations is built in.

The authors set the share of each galaxy’s hydrogen-clearing light that escapes into space at 18%, a value chosen so that hydrogen clears on a realistic schedule. So the timing of that clearing is partly a tuning choice, not a prediction.

The team also slowed the speed of light in the calculation to a fifth of its real value, because the full speed would have made the run unaffordable.

That shortcut may keep hydrogen fog in remote voids a little too long. And the detailed comparison with real quasar spectra, the one that would say whether the helium timing is right, is still to come.

Zier’s team plans to release the full Lumina data in 2028. Companion studies are already using it to work out how patchy clearing marks the afterglow of the Big Bang, and how many quasars of each brightness the early universe held.

Observations from Webb and future surveys by the Roman Space Telescope will help astronomers test whether Lumina can explain how the earliest massive galaxies formed.

The full study was published in the journal Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

During a month-long excavation with the documentary series "Time Team," archaeologists unearthed another mysterious "sand body" at Sutton Hoo.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have discovered a mysterious "sand body" at Sutton Hoo, an Anglo-Saxon cemetery in the U.K. that's famous for an enormous seventh-century ship burial of an early medieval king. The unusual grave does not have any bones but rather ghost-like shapes where a body was once buried.

Sand bodies were "burials where the bodies and bones had dissolved away in the acid soil, replaced by hard sand which held the form of the person, not unlike some of the bodies at Pompeii," Angus Wainwright, an archaeologist at the U.K.'s National Trust, said in a statement. These burials have been found at Sutton Hoo in the past, as well as at other Anglo-Saxon sites in the Suffolk area of the U.K.

The new sand burial, which was uncovered at a burial ground called Garden Field at the end of a 2025 dig, features in a four-part documentary created by the television series "Time Team" and archaeological experts with the National Trust and FAS Heritage. Whereas a 2024 excavation unearthed pieces of a bronze bucket used in a cremation ritual, the 2025 excavation was aimed at discovering evidence for the extent of the cemetery, when it was used and whether the people buried there were connected with the occupant of the famous ship burial.

"Until now, archaeologists have focused on the royal burial mounds," Wainwright said. In particular, experts have tried to work out who was buried in the "great ship burial" at Sutton Hoo. That person may have been King Rædwald, who ruled a kingdom in East Anglia and died around A.D. 627. The ship burial also contained an intricate and striking helmet. But the archaeologists are trying to learn more about the everyday East Anglians with the 2025 dig, which "moves the focus to these people and their ancestors and descendants," Wainwright said.

During the last week of the month-long excavation, the team unearthed the unusual sand body burial. Accompanying the deceased were grave goods, including beads, tweezers, a knife and a brooch, according to the statement. But directly underneath the sand body, the team found evidence that a second person may have been buried in the same grave.

"It was certainly a high point of this latest dig, to find another of these bodies in the Garden Field cemetery," Wainwright said. Experts think the sand bodies and cremations discovered in the burial ground may predate the famous ship burial.

In the first episode of a four-part Time Team series on Sutton Hoo, which launched on YouTube on Nov. 14, experts found new evidence that the people buried in the Garden Field cemetery were acquiring wealth and increasing their social status — so much so that they buried at least one person with a gold ingot.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The team also investigated the possible remains of a dock that was used to build and launch ships into the River Deben and found an unusual fragment of a cremation urn that surprised the archaeologists because it was decorated rather than plain.

"Well, it's at Sutton Hoo. Anything can happen," Justin Garner-Lahire, managing director at FAS Heritage, said in the video.

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6352. The wildlife trade is bigger than previously thought, with nearly 80,000 species and counting

A new review finds that global wildlife trade reaches far beyond familiar pets and seafood, and gaps in recordkeeping make its full scale hard to measure.

Ask about the wildlife trade and most people picture smuggled ivory, tiger skins and pangolins. Almost none of the recorded trade is like that.

Most documented wildlife trade is legal, and it includes the fish in the freezer aisle, the orchid on the windowsill, and the gecko in the pet shop window.

A new review documented 79,554 species in international wildlife trade, well above the roughly 50,000 previously estimated.

A broader tally that included species people use for subsistence and other purposes reached 107,356.

Even the new number is likely a considerable underestimate, the authors wrote, because almost no country records what it buys and sells.

Alice Hughes, a conservation scientist at the University of Melbourne, led the review. Her co-authors come from the organizations that track wildlife trade, including TRAFFIC, the IUCN and the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization.

The count comes from stitching together databases built for other purposes, and the plant half of it rests on records of use rather than records of sale.

In an interview with Earth.com, Hughes said the finding is about ordinary buyers as much as smugglers.

“Almost all of us are part of wildlife trade, and whilst some of that, such as fisheries are managed, sectors like the pet trade are not,” she said.

Legal wildlife trade is worth an estimated $220 billion to $300 billion a year. Smuggled wildlife is worth an estimated $28 billion to $40 billion.

So the legal side is roughly six to 11 times larger than the smuggling that gets the attention.

“When we think of wildlife trade we tend to think about the illegal trade of elephants, tigers and pangolins. But it’s much more than that,” Hughes said.

“Wildlife trade includes everything from timber, seafood and medicinal plants to pets, cut flowers, ornamental fish and fungi, and most of it is legal.”

Legal doesn’t mean harmless. Where researchers have population numbers for a traded species, the populations being collected from are, on average, 50% to 60% smaller than populations left alone.

By one estimate the authors cite, trade has contributed, directly or indirectly, to the global extinction of 294 species.

The team pulled together every trade record it could reach. The largest was the CITES Trade Database, which holds the records of legal trade in protected species going back to 1975.

Alongside it went the IUCN Red List, UN fish and timber records, TRAFFIC’s seizure reports and the US import database.

Beyond the databases, the researchers drew on published surveys of individual animal groups and a world checklist of plants that people use.

Animals accounted for 47,685 species, and up to 31,306 of those are vertebrates. That works out to 42% of every vertebrate species science has described.

Put another way, two out of every five kinds of animal with a backbone have been traded somewhere.

For birds, the share is higher still: about 65% of all living bird species have been traded. Plants and fungi added 59,671 species potentially used or traded.

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service logs wild animal shipments into and out of the United States in a database called LEMIS, and it periodically releases the records.

Since 2000, more than 21,000 wild animal species have been traded into the US alone.

More than a quarter of all traded animal species appear in that one country’s records and in no other database. For mammals, the figure is 54%.

Much of what the world knows about which animals are traded comes from one country’s import records.

Hughes’s team surveyed 61 countries and searched for “wildlife trade database” in 30 languages. The US system was the only full, public record of trade across groups of animals from any country.

“The United States is the only country that systematically records and publicly shares trade data across a wide range of taxa. For much of the rest of the world, equivalent data simply does not exist,” Hughes said.

Asked what it would take for other countries to follow, Hughes told Earth.com it starts with accepting that “legal trade is not necessarily sustainable.”

Without data on trade in other groups, she said, the trade can’t be managed to make sure it is sustainable.

“Trade has changed, the exotic pet trade will continue to grow, and with so many species in trade, that poses a real risk unless we start monitoring it better,” she said.

The pet trade is where the new counts diverge most from the old global estimates. The gaps are largest for reptiles, invertebrates and plants, which are also the hardest to track.

A lizard or a beetle bought online travels by mail and often isn’t identified to species at the border.

CITES, the treaty that regulates trade in at-risk species, covers about 9.5% of reptile species. The new review recorded 4,620 reptile species in trade, about 37% of all described reptiles.

Asked which traded species surprised her most, Hughes said it was how quickly newly described species appear for sale.

Collectors sometimes use the scientific descriptions themselves to find animals to trade, she said. She also pointed to “the price people are willing to pay for some, like 100s of dollars for a single isopod (woodlouse).”

For buyers, Hughes said the place to start is where an animal came from.

Corn snakes and leopard geckos should be captive bred, she said, and chameleons often come from the wild and don’t survive well in captivity.

“If you are not sure where they come from, just don’t buy them, for every wild caught animal in the shop, many others die in transit,” she said.

Governments have agreed on a set of global biodiversity targets, and one of them covers the impacts of trade.

Its single headline measure is the share of fish stocks being fished at sustainable levels. By the review’s count, that measure reflects about 2% of the species in use and trade.

“While the global biodiversity framework does have a target on trade, based on our estimates it only accounts for around two or three percent of species in trade and misses the other 97 percent,” Hughes said.

The authors wrote that the fix doesn’t need a new system. Almost every country already runs customs checks and animal health checks on imports, and most CITES permits are still paper.

Electronic permits exist, but only about 30 of the 184 CITES countries use them.

If customs offices digitized shipping invoices and matched them to a species list, the authors wrote, they would record much of what is now lost.

The United Kingdom has required an electronic tag on every sheep, and a log of its movements, since 2009, so record-keeping on that scale is already being done.

Seizure records reflect how hard a country enforces its laws as much as how much is smuggled. And the databases don’t agree with one another on which species are traded, which is part of the paper’s point.

Even so, Hughes said the estimate is still an underestimate, because most countries do not collect the data.

The larger question is whether wild populations can sustain the trade. An IUCN working group has assessed the potential sustainability of trade for 347 species across 117 countries.

For many traded species, researchers still lack the data to tell how much is being taken from the wild and how those populations are faring.

Hughes and her co-authors propose standardizing how trade data are collected and starting at a regional level, with the European Union as a possible first model.

Until that happens, each new database that opens is likely to add species to the count.

For many species, researchers still can’t tell how trade is affecting wild populations.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#6351. Florida’s invasive pythons don’t always stay on the ground, and about 1 in 7 adult sightings were up in trees

A USGS study found that invasive Burmese pythons in Florida sometimes climb trees, especially in winter, raising concerns for nesting birds.

Burmese pythons invading southern Florida are not primarily tree-dwellers, but some of them climb. Among 188 radio-tracked adults, about 14 percent, or roughly 1 in 7, were found in a tree or shrub at least once, according to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS).

For 168 juveniles, the share was about 17 percent. Across more than 4,000 observations, however, fewer than 3 percent placed a python in a tree or shrub.

Both age groups were most likely to climb in December and January, the cooler months of southern Florida’s dry season.

Each observation came from locating a snake through radio telemetry, not from a chance sighting. Tracking ran from November 2017 to December 2024 in Big Cypress National Preserve.

Lisa McBride, a biologist at the USGS Fort Collins Science Center, is the study’s first author.

A public USGS data release lists 112 tracking events in trees or shrubs, involving 56 different pythons.

The first python was observed in the Everglades in 1979, but no more were seen until 1995. The species now breeds in the preserve and is spreading through south Florida.

Burmese pythons, one of Florida’s invasive reptiles, are notoriously difficult to find. By some estimates, the probability of detecting an individual python can be less than 5 percent.

Adults in trees were seen basking, resting, brooding eggs or gathering with other pythons. Juveniles rested, basked or moved between tree limbs.

Most adults found in trees during the peak climbing months were basking, a behavior that lets reptiles absorb heat from their surroundings.

The researchers suggest pythons may use trees and shrubs at that time of year to maintain a high body temperature.

In February 2022, one adult male basked atop a Brazilian peppertree about 16 feet (5 meters) above the ground. It then climbed to the crown of a cabbage palm, about 23 feet (7 meters) up.

A female brooded her eggs in a fallen, hollow cypress tree about 6.5 feet (2 meters) above the ground in May 2022.

A juvenile female rested on a pond apple tree about 5 feet (1.5 meters) up that same May.

A USGS video shows a juvenile female moving across the branches of a dahoon holly tree in the preserve.

The higher share among juveniles may reflect an ontogenetic shift, a change in habitat use as an animal grows, the researchers suggest.

The probability of finding a python in a tree generally fell as its weight rose. Smaller snakes may move through branches more easily than heavy adults.

Still, trees with strong branches, such as Brazilian peppertrees and live oaks, supported some of the largest pythons tracked.

Adults caught in Florida average 6 to 9 feet (1.8 to 2.7 meters), according to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC). The species can reach 19 feet (5.8 meters), however.

Native from India to lower China, the Malay Peninsula and some islands of the East Indies, Burmese pythons are semi-aquatic and excellent climbers.

The exact route of their introduction is unknown. Pythons likely escaped from a breeding facility destroyed during Hurricane Andrew, and pet pythons have likely been released in and around the Everglades.

The months when adult pythons were most likely to be in trees overlap with the nesting season of several wading-bird species. Earlier studies documented pythons preying on nests of great egrets and white ibises in the Everglades.

No python was seen preying on birds in trees during the tracking. The USGS cautioned that the overlap does not mean tree use is causing bird declines.

Rather, it identifies another behavior that could bring an invasive predator into contact with vulnerable animals, and an area for continued research.

More than 25 percent of captured pythons have birds in their stomachs.

Before 2000, mammals were encountered frequently during nocturnal road surveys in Everglades National Park. Road surveys from 2003 to 2011 then recorded a 99.3 percent drop in raccoon observations as pythons spread.

Opossum observations fell by 98.9 percent and bobcat observations by 87.5 percent. The same surveys failed to detect rabbits.

Some reports put the south Florida python population anywhere from 5,000 to 180,000 snakes, though the best estimates so far place it closer to 30,000.

Almost 28,000 wild Burmese pythons have been removed from Florida’s environment and reported to the FWC since 2000. The 2026 Florida Python Challenge alone removed 280, with 907 participants from 30 U.S. states, Canada and Vietnam.

The South Florida Water Management District also pays agents an hourly rate to hunt pythons. They earn $50 for each snake up to 4 feet (1.2 meters), $25 for each additional foot (0.3 meters) and $200 for each verified active nest.

Seasonal data on tree use “could improve the effectiveness of removal efforts by management agencies,” the authors wrote.

Knowing when pythons climb could also help scientists understand how the snakes interact with the Greater Everglades ecosystem.

The study was published in the journal Journal of Herpetology.

#6350. An El Niño amped by climate change has California bracing for the worst

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Warming has intensified El Niño’s impacts on weather around the globe, making it harder to prepare

Large waves, driven eastward by the strengthening El Niño in the eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, battered the city of Oceanside California (shown) on October 9.

In parts of California, public officials are going door-to-door, warning residents to get ready. The state has strategically stockpiled sandbags, pumps and generators. Debris has been fished out to clear storm drains, seepage blankets shore up aging levees and dams, and wire mesh cages hold back precariously placed boulders.

What is expected to be the strongest El Niño on record is already pounding the state with giant waves. The fury of this year’s El Niño is being unleashed around the globe as well, from inundating Florida with floods to exacerbating drought in the Amazon. And much more is still to come, forecasts show, with the peak of the climate phenomenon expected to arrive between November 2026 and January 2027.

Californians know all too well the threat. El Niño has historically brought relentless rainfall to the state, flooding cities and triggering landslides.

State officials learned a lot about preparedness and emergency water management from previous El Niños — particularly the strong event that spanned the winter of 1997–1998. But this year’s event is likely to be even more challenging, a “Super” El Niño superimposed on the backdrop of global climate change.

Climate change has made water management in California more complicated than it was just 30 years ago — as it has elsewhere around the world, says environmental scientist Letitia Grenier, the director of water policy at the Public Policy Institute of California, a nonprofit, nonpartisan think tank based in San Francisco.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

In 1997, California’s overall climate was much drier; El Niño brought a big, long rainy season that spanned the state, Grenier says. But now, “it’s just so humid. The air is warmer, so it can hold more water.”

That waterlogged atmosphere means that even without El Niño, there’s been less of a distinct rainy season in California, and more rapid flip-flop between intense episodes of rain dumped on the ground followed by periods of heat and dryness. “It’s these strange, erratic patterns that we’ve never seen before,” she says. And the state is bracing for how the Super El Niño will clash with this new climate normal.

1997 was the year that the term “El Niño” shot to global fame. It was the most powerful El Niño in recorded history, and the first to be scientifically monitored in real time, continuously tracked by satellites and breathlessly reported on by news outlets. El Niño’s rise to household name status was even cemented in pop culture by an appearance on Saturday Night Live, in a classic sketch by comedian Chris Farley.

But the event was no laughing matter. It caused global devastation during its brief reign. El Niño events form as westward-blowing trade winds over the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean weaken, allowing warm water to accumulate at the surface. Those waters can then release massive amounts of heat to the atmosphere, altering the position of the Pacific jet stream and helping to disrupt global weather patterns.

In 1997–1998, global temperatures spiked by 1.5 degrees Celsius on average. Along with the torrential rains in California, the event brought brutal drought to Southeast Asia and deadly summer floods to central Europe and Peru. Record-breaking floods also hit East Africa, which in turn triggered a surge in mosquito-borne Rift Valley fever. The oceans were so warm that 16 percent of the world’s reefs died.

In all, the El Niño–related weather extremes were linked to more than 22,000 fatalities around the world, including nearly 200 in the United States, and an estimated $5.7 trillion in global economic losses.

Not every El Niño is equally intense, or impacts weather in quite the same way. “There’s a lot of variability event to event,” says Washington, D.C.–based climate scientist Tom Di Liberto, of the nonprofit climate news organization Climate Central.

But there is a general overall pattern to how El Niño tends to affect weather around the planet, Di Liberto says. For example, there tend to be more tropical cyclones in the Pacific Ocean, and fewer in the Atlantic — a pattern also observed in 2026.

El Niño also tends to flatten and accelerate the Pacific jet stream, shifting its flow southward, says Mike Anderson, California’s state climatologist for the Department of Water Resources, who is based in Sacramento.  And that has historically meant that a conveyor belt of back-to-back moisture-loaded storms is set on a collision course with the U.S. West Coast.

The El Niño rapidly strengthened during the summer of 2026. As westerly trade winds weakened, warm waters accumulated in the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, raising both ocean temperatures and the sea level height (shown in this animation). Red and white colors indicate the highest sea level. Beginning in April and intensifying through November, the El Niño event generated Kelvin waves, massive swells that sweep eastward along the equator toward the Americas.

The 1997–1998 El Niño revealed just how devastating that pattern could be in California.

As much as 30 centimeters inundated parts of the state during the month of February 1998 alone. Storm winds and high surf pounded the coast, while rivers swelled and overtopped their banks. Flooding from the “Groundhog Day Storm” destroyed some 1,700 homes in Bay Area cities Palo Alto and Menlo Park. On February 6 near Rio Nido, about 100 kilometers from San Francisco, a forested hillside suddenly crumbled, sending a wall of mud rushing down the mountain. It destroyed about 30 homes.

Landslides also threatened homes and lives in Southern California.

On February 23, then 25-year-old Jenifer Segraves and her fiancé Glenn Flook were living in an apartment on Laguna Canyon Road, in the city of Laguna Beach. The heavy rains had saturated the neighborhood’s steep hillsides, making the terrain unstable.

“We lived up against a hill in the canyon, so there were stairs up to our apartment,” Segraves says now. “They became like a waterfall. I remember my fiancé carrying me up the stairs because there was so much water.” Segraves called her father, Gary Segraves, in a panic, asking for help. Then, the slope behind the building failed, the apartment flooded and she and Flook fled into the rushing mud.

“We were strong enough to get out, but we were waist-high in mud,” Segraves said. “[My dad] almost drowned getting to us.” All three took shelter at a neighbor’s house, where they showered and hunkered down to wait out the rain.

Around midnight on February 24, the second mudslide arrived.

The neighbor’s “whole house went down,” Segraves says. She escaped through a second-floor window, but her fiancé fell through the floor and was knocked out. He didn’t make it out.

Gary Segraves, meanwhile, was swept down the hillside and landed in a pile of rubble against a rocky cliff. Battered and missing his glasses, he looked around and saw what looked like a doll.

He reached for the little form — and discovered that it was a baby, very cold but alive. Somehow, the 9-month-old had survived being swept out of her crib from a nearby home. The little girl “wouldn’t have survived if he hadn’t picked her up,” Segraves says.

The havoc wreaked across California by the event 30 years ago cast a stark light on the desperate need to expand waterways, maintain infrastructure and coordinate emergency services, Grenier says. “An engineering system can only work as well as its capacity.”

Much of the state’s infrastructure is deteriorating. An October 13 report by the California state auditor noted that the condition of dams and levees across the state “remains a high-risk issue,” with some 57 dams in the state in poor or unsatisfactory condition. “Poorly maintained dams and levees continue to pose a risk to public safety,” the report said.

California’s water management system was also originally designed specifically to simply shunt excess water away from residential areas, rather than try to capture the water or help it infiltrate into aquifers, Grenier says. But that system worked for a different climate, one that wasn’t so prone to “weather whiplash” — wild, sudden swings between extremely wet and extremely dry conditions.

Alongside punishing, drenching back-to-back storms called atmospheric rivers, the state has also experienced frequent episodes of drought, including two recent severe events, one lasting from 2012 to 2016 and another from 2021 to 2025.

Those years of drought, dwindling snow and pumping too much water from aquifers have dramatically depleted the state’s subsurface water stores. And the heavy rains don’t necessarily help; the torrents of water mostly run off across the surface instead of infiltrating soils to reach the underground aquifer.

Such hydroclimate whiplash isn’t unique to California by any means. It’s a global problem, and it’s becoming more common. A small increase in air temperatures can give a big boost to the atmosphere’s capacity to hold water vapor, increasing that capacity by about 7 percent for every 1 degree C of temperature increase. All of that water vapor has contributed to an increase in extreme precipitation events around the globe since the mid-20th century.

Precipitation is just half of the problem. Rising air temperatures also make the air “thirstier,” causing it to draw even more moisture out of vegetation, soil and surface bodies of water during drier periods — which makes the land more vulnerable to severe drought and wildfire.

It’s now clear that these hydrodynamic shifts have been increasing the frequency of weather whiplash events around the world over the last 75 years or so, scientists reported in 2025. And that whiplash is likely to increase as the world warms more.

Months before reaching peak intensity, the 2026–2027 Super El Niño has begun making its presence known. The Amazon is suffering under intense heat and drought, priming the region for wildfires and pushing the forest closer to a worrisome possible fate: a transition from tropical forest to savanna grasslands. Fires have also begun blazing across Southeast Asia, while heavy rains began inundating the Horn of Africa in October. Arriving on the heels of severe drought, that one-two punch could devastate the region’s crops and pasturelands.

In California, the first harbingers of the arrival of the Super El Niño appeared in early September. Heavy surf pounded the coastline. Regions from San Francisco to Los Angeles saw record high tides by late October that flooded city streets and battered coastlines and seawalls, even as the skies remained clear.

The waves were amped up by an unfortunate trifecta: higher sea levels due to climate change; a lunar cycle that exerted its maximum pull on the tides; and an El Niño–linked phenomenon called Kelvin waves.

Kelvin waves are massive, slow-moving swells of warm ocean water, part of the complicated interplay between wind and water that produces the El Niño Southern Oscillation, the overall weather pattern that includes El Niño and counterpart La Niña events, says Josh Willis, an oceanographer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif.

As prevailing west-blowing winds weaken over the tropical eastern Pacific, Willis says, water normally pushed west by the winds instead sloshes back eastward. Kelvin waves have historically given a boost to sea levels along the U.S. West Coast of as much as 30 centimeters. This year, that impact could be larger, researchers reported September 30 in a preprint study posted on EarthArXiv.org. Computer model simulations suggest that the risk of the risk of extreme sea levels could be 10 times higher during this El Niño year than during previous events, for coastlines from Alaska all the way to Chile.

Then, by late October, the Santa Ana winds arrived: Hot, dry gusts blowing down the mountains toward the coast, fanning wildfires in Southern California. The fires scarred the landscape, denuding it of vegetation, roots that helped stabilize and fortify the soil. Such loosened soil is more likely to become mobilized into a debris flow during heavy rains.

Those rains are now on the way. By mid-November, researchers began tracking storms headed for California. The peak of El Niño is expected to arrive by late November or early December and persist through February or March.

Segraves, after surviving nearly 30 years ago, says she is aware that another El Niño is coming. But she hasn’t been following the news closely. She’s placed herself on a news diet since her ordeal. She refused to speak to media for years, or even read the coverage about her own story.

“Everyone wanted to talk to me and I just wanted to be left alone,” she says. Staying away from the news “freed me from all that. It changed my view on life. I take each day as it comes.”

But, she adds, one lesson has stayed with her. “I swore I would never live on a cliff again.”
