#6212. Airline Captain Defends 20-Year-Old Female Copilot After Fatal Learjet Crash

121pilot, our resident commercial airline pilot on Live And Let’s Fly, examines what we know about the crash of Learjet 60 N722BD and pushes back against the rush to blame its young first officer, Nathalia Filgueiras.

The crash of N722BD, a Learjet 60 operating on a charter flight, has drawn enormous attention. Much of that is understandable. We have extremely dramatic video of the aircraft descending almost vertically at a very high rate of speed, along with equally dramatic ATC audio recordings.

As is typical of the aviation YouTube community, many of whom I respect, people have been rushing to get videos out about this accident. What I really don’t care for, however, are the clickbait titles. Titles like “Could Any Pilot Have Saved This Learjet 60?” or “Lear 60 Florida Crash: It Happened Before” or “Expert Pilot Explains What Likely Caused SHOCKING Plane Crash in Florida” by Megyn Kelly.

These kinds of titles make me angry because, regardless of the actual content of the videos, they are misleading. The simple fact is that we know very little about this accident at this point, and certainly not enough to be speculating about a probable cause.

The aircraft, a Learjet Model 60 with nine people aboard, reported moderate turbulence and icing at Flight Level 350 and requested a climb to Flight Level 370. Moments later, the aircraft departed controlled flight, eventually entering a descent at an extraordinarily high rate of speed.

We know that the NTSB has recovered components of the horizontal stabilizer that separated from the aircraft, and widely circulated video appears to show the aircraft without this crucial component.

What we DON’T know is whether the aircraft flew into a thunderstorm. The weather imagery I’ve seen to date comes from sources that have time lags built into them and don’t necessarily represent the real-time weather picture. We don’t know what caused the horizontal stabilizer to separate, or even when that happened. Did it separate during the dive, or was its failure what initiated the dive? That’s an important distinction, and right now it’s an unknown.

We know the Learjet 60’s wing is sensitive to ice accumulation and that the aircraft is susceptible to a phenomenon called Mach tuck. We don’t know whether either played any role in this accident, or even whether the aircraft’s critical surfaces had accumulated ice.

We know the aircraft had been operating at higher altitudes, with a reported descent from Flight Level 410 to 350 before the final sequence of events. But without knowing the aircraft’s speed, configuration, weight, and other performance parameters, we cannot draw meaningful conclusions about its operating margins.

We know the captain was 55 years old and very experienced. We know the first officer was 20 years old and relatively inexperienced, but fully qualified to act as a second in command.

We know the CVR, or cockpit voice recorder, has been recovered, but we don’t yet know whether its contents can be successfully recovered or what information it might provide. We also know the aircraft was not equipped with a flight data recorder, or FDR. That means information about the aircraft’s speed, heading, pitch, roll, system status, and other parameters may remain unknown or will have to be reconstructed using external data sources and whatever information can be gleaned from the CVR.

But perhaps the most disturbing part of this entire event, aside from the tragic loss of life, has been the reaction of so many people who couldn’t explain the difference between a slat and a flap, yet have felt perfectly qualified to judge the performance of the first officer based on her age and gender.

In the Megyn Kelly video, she questions whether someone who isn’t even old enough to drink should have been acting as a pilot.

I think the better question is why we allow 18-year-olds to join the military and go into combat, but apparently don’t think they’re old enough to have a beer. Why can a 20-year-old warrant officer fly a Black Hawk full of troops into the maelstrom of a hot landing zone, but we think he or she can’t be trusted with alcohol?

Even more disgusting have been some of the reactions to the ATC recordings.

First, let me suggest that if you haven’t already listened to them, don’t. Second, and most importantly, as a 56-year-old male airline captain, I hear absolutely nothing in that recording, either in her voice or in her actions, that merits criticism.

I don’t think people who haven’t experienced it can appreciate just how incredibly violent and terrifying that initial descent must have been. In one recording, we go from a seemingly calm situation, with the crew requesting a climb, to a loss of control and a reported descent of approximately 8,000 feet per minute in about 10 seconds. Just 16 seconds later, the aircraft is in an overspeed condition, and the first officer reports a descent rate of 20,000 feet per minute. That’s an absolutely eye-watering number. It defies belief and would be utterly terrifying to any pilot. About 10 seconds later, she reports that they are going to crash into the ground. Not long after that, someone can be heard in the background reciting the Lord’s Prayer.

I don’t know this for certain, of course, but my suspicion is that somewhere during this sequence the crew became aware that the horizontal stabilizer had separated and that they had lost the ability to recover the aircraft.

If there is anything to be said about her performance as a pilot, it’s that she was clearly doing her job right up to the end.

We teach Aviate, Navigate, Communicate. Aviate means flying the airplane. Navigate means determining where you need to go and how to get there. Communicate means keeping the appropriate people informed.

In this situation, the captain was presumably concentrating on flying the aircraft while the first officer was communicating with ATC. That is exactly what we expect from a two-person crew in an emergency, assuming those were their respective roles at the time.

What’s more, in the absence of an FDR, the information she provided to ATC may prove absolutely crucial to understanding what happened. We may eventually discover that her actions and communications were instrumental in allowing the NTSB to piece together this accident. That information could well save lives in the future.

I also find it interesting, and troubling, that contrary to the media’s usual fixation on the captain, as though he’s flying the airplane solo, the exact opposite has happened here. The first officer has become the focus of an extraordinary amount of attention, even though we have not established who was flying the aircraft.

It’s been my absolute privilege to fly with a number of female pilots throughout my career, and not one of them has ever done anything less than a sterling job. Frankly, the airplane doesn’t care about your gender or the color of your skin. And when it comes to aviation, that’s exactly how it should be. We should care about qualifications and competence. That’s it.

If I step onto my jet tomorrow and find a young female first officer waiting for me, I’ll be just as happy to have her there as I would a young male. At this point in my career, flying with a young and relatively inexperienced first officer gives me the opportunity to act as a mentor and pass along some hard-won flying wisdom. That’s something I genuinely enjoy. Nathalia had earned her place in that cockpit. Not one iota of the solid evidence we have right now leads me to believe that this accident can or should be blamed on her.

It may well turn out that crew errors figure prominently in the probable cause. We simply don’t know yet. But if that turns out to be the case, it’s important to remember that the captain was the pilot in command. He was responsible for the operation of that aircraft, and the first officer was serving under his command. If poor decision-making put the aircraft into a situation from which there was no escape, the captain would bear the primary responsibility for those decisions.

But that’s a hypothetical. And right now, we don’t know that any such decisions were made.

We owe the nine people who lost their lives, their families, and the people who will eventually investigate this accident something better than speculation, sensationalism, and a rush to judgment.

121pilot is a pilot for a major U.S. commercial airline who offers analysis on industry news as well as occasional reflections on his own travels.

Yeah, no. There was no excuse for these pilots to thread the needle between two storm systems and risk safety in the process. Both overestimated the capabilities of their aircraft, one known to be prone to the issues experienced and proved fatal.

From a legal standpoint, the author is correct. We don’t know. However we have a reasonable scenario that is worth trying to prevent in the future….. icing conditions caused a dive which shredded the horizontal stabilizer in the back if the plane sending it into an unrecoverable dive.

Nope. A 20 year old should NEVER be the first officer. When DEI virtue signaling replaces common sense, bad things happen. Case in point. This is an absolute tragedy for all parties involved, but I never ever ever want a 20 year old at the controls (male or female). And to all the usual suspects (commenters like 1990, etc), I don’t want to hear the nonsense about age and military comparisons. The training of Air Force / Naval aviators is exponentially deeper than what we are talking about here. It’s like saying ‘I can drive a Toyota Corolla around the corner” to an F1 driver.

The issue here is not that she was female. The issue is that it was a very young co-pilot who showed signs of immaturity and questionable professional standards, not exactly surprising considering she was 20 years old. The comparison to Army helicopter pilots has some validity but less than you think. The Army is a very disciplined environment and certain things would simply not be tolerated that might be at a small charter operation. This is a chronic problem at the small, low paid charter companies. They have trouble retaining people who leave as soon as they can move up the ladder. So they have to replace them with whoever they can get. There is a term for the replacements, “seat fillers,” meaning people who lack the background and experience to do the job at a high level.

This is not an issue at places like NetJets, which is the largest charter operator and a career job. Good pay, benefits, schedules and a top notch training department. They get more than enough applications from very experienced pilots. They don’t have 20 year olds coming from Cessna 150s flying their aircraft.

This co-pilot was texting with her boyfriend ten minutes before the accident. They weren’t in clear air. They were dodging thunderstorms and dealing with ice. If there is ever a time for a pilot to be 100% focused on the task at hand, that is it.

This was not her first rodeo with ATC. The situation in the video linked at the bottom occurred a few months ago in New York. The basic knowledge about turbulence and how to report it to ATC is lacking. Chop and turbulence have different meanings. Moderate and severe turbulence have specific definitions and she did not understand it. Her response to the exasperated controller, “We were about to call you” is more like the language of a teenager than a professional pilot.

We will likely never know definitively why this accident happened. The aircraft was picking up ice but that should have been manageable with the deicing system. Was it turned on and if so, was it turned on early enough? They entered a climb but was it done too abruptly, causing them to stall the plane? Was it something else we don’t know?

They definitely entered a thunderstorm and would have had it painting on their radar for some time. Time lag is a non-issue here. But was the radar used correctly? The Lear 60 doesn’t have multi-scan radar as standard equipment and I doubt it was installed later. This means that the tilt control had to be operated manually. Manual tilt works very well but it takes some knowledge and experience to use properly.

Regardless of the cause, the ultimate responsibilty for everything that happens rests with the Captain. But crew experience, training and proficiency are always part of the puzzle that the investigation will look at.

I once was flying down to Cozumel on a beautiful, clear January morning. Smooth air and nothing but a few high puffy clouds. We were about 200 miles from the island and already saw on the radar that Cozumel had nothing painting in the area. The regional pilot (a male, btw) told the startled Mexican controller that they would have to hold because there was a thunderstorm over the airport. The controller asked incredulously about there being a thunderstorm there and the crew responded affirmitively. There was a pause and the controller came back and said Cozumel Tower says there is no storm at the airport. The regional crew eventually accepted this and continued. We had a good chuckle and figured the likely cause was that the regional had the radar selected to manual mode with the tilt too low, so they were painting a return of the island itself and thinking it was a thunderstorm. Sh*t happens out there, even to old pilots, and we all learn from our mistakes, 🙂

#6209. Sweet: Deaf 5-Year-Old Bonds With American Airlines Flight Attendant And Gets A Surprise Welcome From CEO

A flight attendant signing with a young passenger is a lovely moment on its own. But seeing five-year-old Luca meet American Airlines CEO Robert Isom, who learned a few signs to greet him, made me smile even more. We spend plenty of time examining what airlines get wrong. Here is something American got right.

Luca is five years old, Deaf, and loves airplanes. In a video shared by American Airlines, a flight attendant communicates with him in sign language near the aircraft door and. again onboard. Watching Luca respond is delightful.

There is something particularly sweet about seeing a child discover that someone outside his family can communicate with him in his own language. The flight attendant takes the time to engage with Luca directly, and his reaction is precious.

The family later shared footage of a visit to American Airlines in Dallas, including a meeting with Isom.

According to his mother, Isom took the time to learn how to spell his name and sign “nice to meet you” in American Sign Language. He also gave Luca American Airlines trading cards, which she said he was very excited about.

Her explanation of why the meeting mattered was simple:

“I can’t tell you how much it means when someone takes that extra step to communicate with him.”

A post shared by CALLIE FOSTER (@thelacouple)

In another post about the visit, she described hundreds of American employees gathering to welcome Luca, with many having learned some sign language for him. She said the family had not known what American had planned and was overwhelmed by the reception.

That is quite a day for a little boy who loves airplanes.

These small gestures make a huge difference…isn’t that true of so many things in life?

Isom could have posed for a photograph, handed over the trading cards, and still called it a successful visit. Instead, he learned enough to introduce himself and greet Luca directly. Taking a little time beforehand allowed him to participate in the conversation rather than leave all the communicating to Luca’s parents.

The same goes for the employees who learned signs before welcoming him. It is easy to talk about the need to “care for people on life’s journey” (the current AA slogan). Here, they did something practical to make that happen.

As a father, I understand why his mother was so touched. When someone makes an effort for your child, you remember it. A brief interaction that an employee might regard as a small part of the workday can become something a family talks about long afterward.

And yes, American shared the encounter on social media. I am glad it did. There is room to recognize good hospitality even when an airline benefits from showing it.

Between the flight attendant signing with Luca and the welcome he received at American’s campus, this family has some wonderful memories to take home. I appreciated watching Isom make the effort too. Learning a greeting is a modest undertaking, but his mother’s account explains how much it meant. Well done to everyone at American who helped make Luca feel so welcome. This was a refreshing bit of airline news to watch.

#6208. Türkiye Just Announced a New Golden Visa Starting at $150,000

Türkiye is one of the world’s most visited countries, straddling the vibrant crossroads of Europe, Asia, and the Middle East. With sun-soaked Mediterranean beaches, Ottoman-influenced gastronomy, historic mosques, and bustling bazaars, it’s no surprise that the country attracted nearly 64 million visitors in 2025. But if your love of the country has you considering a prolonged vacation (or perhaps a second home), the government’s new golden visa might be a good fit—so long as you have $150,000 to spend.

On November 17, Türkiye's president Recep Tayyip Erdoğan signed a decision to enact a new foreign investor visa. The program offers two pathways: a $150,000 investment for a three-year residence permit, or $200,000 for a five-year stay (both of which can extend to the applicant’s spouse and dependents).

As for where your money goes, you can deposit your funds in a local bank, buy government debt instruments, contribute to a pension plan, or invest in real estate or venture capital funds. No matter which pathway you select, you must hold your investment for at least half the visa term (as in, 1.5 years for the three-year visa or 2.5 years for the five-year visa). That means you could potentially withdraw your investment as early as after 18 months, according to IMI Daily, an investment migration trade publication.

The president’s announcement doesn't detail when or how foreigners can begin to apply, or the specific documents required. However, applications for the country’s other residence-by-investment permits require documents such as proof of financial means and health insurance, according to the government’s Investment and Finance Office.

If you don’t want to shell out $150,000, Türkiye offers other (renewable) relocation pathways. You may qualify for a two-year Short-Term Residence Permit for reasons such as tourism and university-sponsored research. Or, if your spouse is Turkish, you could apply for the three-year Family Residence Permit. Once you’ve lived in the country continuously for eight years, you’ll be eligible to apply for the indefinite Long-Term Residence Permit, which grants you almost all the same perks as citizenship, minus civic duties such as the ability to vote and mandatory military service.

It's important to note that the new golden visa does not provide permanent citizenship. If you’re hoping to find your way into a passport, get ready to spend more. Türkiye’s citizenship-by-investment pipeline will require you to buy a home worth at least $400,000, invest at least $500,000 in sectors such as government bonds or venture capital funds, or, alternatively, help create at least 50 jobs.

Over the last few years, the influx of new residency-by-investment programs has made it easier for wealthy travelers to relocate internationally. In New Zealand, you can invest $1 million New Zealand Dollars (about $567,300) in exchange for a three-year work-to-residency track. For Mediterranean living, Greece offers a five-year permit for a 250,000 euro (about $291,120) investment in a startup. Or, for a more affordable option, Paraguay has a permanent residency program for those who can invest $150,000 in “tourism projects” or $200,000 in stocks or real estate—putting it in line with Türkiye as one of the more affordable relocation options.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6207. Biden: ‘Hard to take’ as Pelosi, Schumer turned on him in 2024

President Joe Biden, Speaker Nancy Pelosi, and Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., arrive for The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 bill signing at the White House, on Aug. 9, 2022. In his new memoir, Biden said he was disappointed when Pelosi and Schumer urged him to drop out of the presidential race in 2024. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

In conversations with Democratic strategists in recent months, I heard a strikingly similar sentiment when the topic turned to Joe Biden’s forthcoming memoir. The consensus view, even among some who’d worked for the former president, was that if he did anything other than accept some responsibility for his role in Donald Trump’s return to the White House, they didn’t have much appetite to hear what he had to say about anything else.

Spoiler alert: Biden offers only a full-throated defense of his decision to seek reelection in 2024, and expresses deep disappointment over what he casts as a disloyal pressure campaign orchestrated by party leaders to force him out of the presidential race despite what he cites as his successes in the office.

But while his perspective on the climactic moment of his political career will be the most scrutinized portion of Biden’s new book, “Promise Me, America” seems primarily intended to offer the former president a platform he has otherwise not had since leaving office: to catalog what he sees as his historic achievements and offer his perspective on how he wrestled with the major issues of our time.

It’s often said that the only thing better than being president is being a former president. That has hardly been the case for Biden in the nearly 22 months since he left the White House, especially as he’s endured what his son Hunter has described as “debilitating” physical pain following a cancer diagnosis last March.

But where “Thanks, Obama” became a popular mantra nearly a decade ago for Democrats seeking to defend and celebrate the 44th president’s record in contrast with the first Trump administration, no such widespread nostalgia has emerged around Biden, as the party is loath to revisit the trauma of the summer of 2024.

The sheer length of his new book — more than 400 pages — seems an implicit acknowledgment that presenting a positive portrait of Biden’s single term in office is largely to be a solitary effort. Over 15 chapters, Biden offers sometimes mechanical descriptions of specific policies and their impact, but also new details of the sausage-making required to pass major initiatives like the Inflation Reduction Act. That legislation, he writes, was revived thanks in part to an Italian dinner hosted by Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo to make peace between West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin III and White House Chief of Staff Ron Klain.

Biden writes in sweeping terms about other accomplishments like responding to the COVID-19 crisis he inherited, calling his administration’s work “one of the most monumental achievements in public health history.” He repeatedly defends his frequent efforts to warn Americans about the need to safeguard our democracy even as critics in the press and his own party suggested he focus more on economic concerns.

Supporting Ukraine in its war against Russia gets the most extensive treatment of any single issue in the book, including a detailed account of Biden’s clandestine trip to Kyiv in February 2023. And the former Senate Foreign Relations Committee chairman takes great effort to delve into the complexity of the U.S.-China relationship and his relationship with President Xi Jinping, while asserting that Taiwan “will likely be the most important foreign policy challenge in the world over the next generation.”

Recurring throughout the book are expressions of optimism that under his administration, Washington was beginning to work again like it was supposed to, that America’s global leadership was being restored through its alliances, and that he was tackling problems that previous presidents had sidestepped. And in offering this comprehensive presentation of his record, Biden also offers his primary rationale for running again.

“We had accomplished so much —  I wanted to finish the job. And yes: I believed I was the best person to do it,” he says. “I was the only person who had ever beaten Donald Trump. And I felt I was the best person to do it again.”

One of Biden’s top advisers put it to me a different way in the months leading up to his decision to seek another term. “He has been running for president for 50 years. And the idea that he would actually be president and stop running for president is almost laughably preposterous.”

The biggest question, of course, was his age, something Biden, who was 81 when he dropped out of the race, asserts he gave serious consideration.

“I knew better than anyone how old I was. I knew what I was —  and wasn’t —  capable of doing. I carefully monitored how I was meeting the demands of the job. And there is not a single example of me failing to handle my responsibilities,” he writes.

The June 27 debate, of course, created a very different perception, as Biden acknowledges that his flubbed comment that “we finally beat Medicare” was to become “Exhibit A that I was too old to do the job.” But he tries to argue it was no different than the poor showings of previous incumbent presidents, including President Barack Obama, in their first debates.

“The difference was that every other president was given the chance to redeem themselves in a second debate. As it turned out, that chance would not be available to me,” Biden writes.

He argues the response he was seeing from voters at his public events after the debate didn’t justify the panicked response of elected Democrats in Washington, and that public polling showed only minor slippage after the debate, until a steady drumbeat of elected Democrats publicly began calling for him to step aside.

Describing separate visits from former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., personally urging him to step aside, he says there was a “yawning gap between what I was seeing with Democratic voters and what I was hearing from the Democratic leadership in Washington.”

“I have to admit it was personally hard to take so many old friends turning on me,” Biden says. “I told Schumer he had a lot of gumption (I may have said it differently at the time), coming to my home and telling me to get out of the race. Loyalty matters to me. If I give you my word, I stick with you. If I say I’m with you, I’m with you to the end.”

At one point, Biden seems to reflect some resentment that some of the Democrats who would ultimately call on him to drop out of the race had themselves been too afraid to challenge him in the first place, saying: “Anyone who was scared off from running has no business being president.” While there was a constant narrative about the weakness of his candidacy, Biden acknowledges, the lack of a serious challenger was in fact a sign of his strength.

“I had it on good authority that several big names in Democratic politics had looked at running. They held meetings and took polls and talked to donors and to potential staff. If they thought I was weak or vulnerable, they would have taken their shot. But they didn’t,” he writes.

Biden’s defiant tone, and his insistence that the lack of party unity was a greater threat to his continued candidacy than his own performance, may be dismissed by Democrats who don’t want to revisit this difficult chapter. But as Schumer and other Democratic leaders are now facing their own internal challenges, “Promise Me, America” may also serve as a cautionary note for an ambitious crop of potential candidates hoping to reclaim the presidency in 2028.

#6206. Report: Lufthansa to Cut 1,000 Jobs

Lufthansa Group plans to lay off around 1,000 full-time workers at its flagship carrier as elevated fuel prices and service disruptions continue to undercut earnings.

The airline group disclosed the cuts in a letter sent to employees and seen by Dow Jones Newswire, according to The Wall Street Journal. The reductions will target Lufthansa’s hubs in Frankfurt and Munich.

Company leaders said their 2024 turnaround plan, initially expected to boost earnings by €2.5 billion over four years, is no longer enough to keep the brand on solid financial ground.

“The year 2026 has set us back: the war in the Middle East, the still very high fuel costs, nine days of strike action, and our already very high cost base have intensified the situation,” the letter said.

Lufthansa failed to reach an agreement with its pilot union earlier this week, setting the stage for a possible work stoppage. The impasse has already resulted in two short strikes, one in February, the other in March.

Lufthansa Group has spoken openly about the damage caused by higher fuel prices over the last nine months. Over the summer, it retired aircraft, cut routes, and warned that layoffs were likely unless prices eased.

According to EuroNews, Lufthansa has lost on average about €20 million per month since the start of the year.

#6205. American Airlines Offers “His” Free First Class Upgrade For $91, Then Tells Frequent Flyer To Delete His Complaint

An American Airlines frequent flyer complained about a $91 first class upgrade offer and received a response asking him to delete his post. That might sound like an airline trying to suppress criticism, but there is a much more sensible explanation: his screenshot exposed his reservation details. As for the inexpensive upgrade itself, I see a pragmatic opportunity rather than a scandal.

This hit my algorithm on X (and apparently VFTW too), but an AAdvantage Executive Platinum member took to the platform to express frustration that American was offering paid first class upgrades for $91 while his complimentary upgrade had not cleared (this was on a short 551-mile flight from Dallas to El Paso).

American acknowledged his frustration, then added:

“Please delete this from public view and join us in DM.”

The response attracted attention, but the screenshot included the passenger’s reservation confirmation number. That is a good reason to remove it and not a sign of AA trying to hide from its transactional upgrade policy!

We can understand why this feels frustrating. Your loyalty is genuinely appreciated, and we're sorry this experience left you feeling overlooked. Please delete this from public view and join us in DM.

— americanair (@AmericanAir) November 18, 2026

It seems obvious to me that American was trying to protect the passenger here.

A reservation confirmation number, often called a record locator or PNR, is something you should keep private. Combined with your last name, it can potentially allow someone to retrieve your booking. Depending on the airline and its security controls, that could expose information about your trip or allow someone to interfere with it. At least with AA you also need your birthdate in order to access the record online or on the AA app.

Posting a screenshot to make a point about upgrades should not mean giving strangers an opportunity to tamper with your reservation…and some losers have far too much on their hand (which I’ve found out the hard way and why even when I “live blog” I never truly live blog).

American could have explained this much better. A simple request to remove the screenshot because it contained private booking information would have avoided the ambiguity. The passenger could then have reposted his complaint with those details obscured.

As to the underlying complaint, I understand why an Executive Platinum member would be frustrated. If you have directed substantial business to an airline and are waiting for an upgrade, watching the airline offer that seat for a relatively small payment can feel like your loyalty counts for very little.

But I am not going to attack American for selling inexpensive upgrades. This is the business model now, and I use it to my advantage when I fly AA. If the economy fare is attractive and American subsequently offers a reasonably priced upgrade, I can evaluate the total cost and decide whether first class is worth it. Sometimes it is. Sometimes I am perfectly happy staying where I am, like on a recent flight where I ended up with an entire row to myself. Oddly, sometimes the cost of the upgrade is more than buying the ticket outright…I have no explanation for that.

That is a much more straightforward transaction than spending more throughout the year in the hope that an airline will eventually reward me with a seat it would still prefer to sell.

Fundamentally, a complimentary upgrade that has not cleared, even at the gate, is not a seat that already belongs to the elite member. We can debate all day long about how prominently or aggressively airlines market upgrades when frequent flyers are waiting when upgrades are dangled like a carrot on a stick, but passengers can respond to that change by reconsidering how much they are willing to spend pursuing status.

I am a free agent, and it is liberating. More people should try it. Two years in, I’m more happy than ever (and flying in first class more than ever on domestic flights). I  choose a flight because the schedule works or because the price makes sense, without worrying that I am depriving my preferred airline of another qualifying flight or dollar toward next year’s status.

If American offers a good fare and an inexpensive first class upgrade, great. I can take advantage of it. I do not need to be an Executive Platinum member to recognize a good deal (as much as I miss the oneworld emerald lounge access when traveling internationally).

That does not mean status has become worthless. I still receive occasional complimentary upgrades as both an American Airlines Gold and United Airlines Gold member. I appreciate those upgrades very much, especially when I am not expecting them. But I do not build my travel plans around them. Hoping for a free upgrade seems futile in many cases even with top-tier status, particularly when the airline business model now centers on actively trying to sell the remaining seats.

For me, an occasional upgrade is a pleasant bonus on a flight I was otherwise willing to fly in economy class on. But upgrades are not a compelling reason to keep spending more with one airline when another offers a better flight….sorry, but the value proposition is gone.

American Airlines could have been clearer about why it wanted this passenger to delete his post. Still, the exposed reservation details provide a sensible explanation, and I would not characterize the request as an attempt to silence criticism.

As for the $91 upgrade, I am pragmatically happy those offers exist. They give me another way to sit up front without organizing my travel around the pursuit of top-tier status. I still enjoy the occasional complimentary upgrade, but choosing flights on my own terms, and paying for a better seat when the price is right, has been far more satisfying than chasing an upgrade that may never clear. Try it, you’ll like it.

#6202. Review: Air France Business Class Lounge – Paris (CDG) – Terminal 2E, Hall L (Now Sans Sauna…)

You can read a more comprehensive review below, but here are some key points:

I’m big fan of this lounge..it’s a nice one even without the controversial sauna. Here are some photos:

> Read More: Air France Closes Paris Lounge Sauna After Passengers Apparently Turned It Into A Sex Den

Although I’ve been to this lounge several times over the years, my last formal review was when it first opened in 2019, which I’ve included as a point of reference below.

I’ve showcased stock photos of the lounge before, but the photos below are all my own. Because the spa in the La Premiere Lounge closed early, I was offered a spa treatment in this new business class lounge. Although it was in a different section of the terminal, I was driven over and did not have to re-clear security.

The lounge is located on the upper level just past the security checkpoint. As you enter the lounge, you’ll be greeted by a moving sign that resembles a glass of champagne.

Since the purpose of my visit to the lounge was to use the spa, let’s start there. Immediately upon arrival I was ushered into a treatment room and given a 15-minute facial. The lady who performed the facial was chatty and gave me a laundry list of cream recommendations, bluntly stating that my face was too dry. Normally, you can sign up for these treatments on a first-come, first-served basis when you reach the lounge. Advance reservations are not permitted.

This lounge is spread out over one (very) large area with couches and chairs scattered throughout the lounge. Perhaps my visit, on December 23rd, was not a typical Saturday evening, but the lounge was less than 1/4 full. The entire rear half of the lounge was virtually empty.

The lounge manager saw I was taking pictures and knew I was a La Premiere passenger, so he beckoned me to follow him into a room marked “Private”. The room, he explained, was reserved for top-tier elites (by request) or special VIP guests.

In the center of the lounge is a beautiful dining room called Le Balcon with velvet couches and brass accents. It serves as a place to eat and a cocktail bar in the evening.

Buffets are stationed throughout the lounge with a selection of beverages and hot and cold food items.

At the far end of the lounge is an open kitchen in which a special dish of the day is prepared.

With the exception of the cocktail bar, alcohol is self-serve and champagne (Laurent Perrier) is available.

Even more than a facial, I would have loved to use the sauna in this lounge. Sadly, a guest had become ill the day before and vomited in it. Thus, it was quarantined pending sterilization. So much for that idea….

> Read More: A New Airport Lounge With A Sauna

Shower suites and restrooms were also available.

(This is a handicapped shower…they do not all look like this).

Next to the Clarins Spa was a rest area with chairs designed for napping. Don’t forget to set your alarm if you use one of these!

In all honesty, I liked this lounge a lot but liked the decor of the Terminal 2E, Hall M lounge better. The dining area / cocktail bar in the center of this lounge is beautiful. Everything else is just nice. Air France offers excellent lounges in Paris that are worth stopping in at before your flight whether you are flying in business class or simply have SkyTeam elite status. Don’t forget to sign up for a complimentary facial or massage…it is worthwhile.

> Read More: Air France Business Class Lounge Paris (CDG) – Terminal 2E, Hall M

#6200. Early Travel Tuesday Deals Are in Motion—Save on Bookings With Expedia, Hyatt, and Celebrity Today

If there's one thing better than having a vacation on the calendar, it's knowing you didn’t pay full price for it. And right on cue, one of the most exciting stretches of the travel-booking year is kicking off. With Thanksgiving around the corner, Travel Tuesday is already making its presence known, bringing early-bird deals on flights, hotels, cruises, and vacation packages for travelers ready to trade their wish lists for boarding passes.

The annual event, which falls on the Tuesday after Thanksgiving—this year, on December 1—has become a prime moment for savvy travelers to score booking discounts, whether that’s a Caribbean beach escape in the depths of winter, a European summer adventure, or simply a long weekend somewhere new.

The best part? You don't have to wait until the official Travel Tuesday date to start saving. Airlines and hotel groups are getting a head start with early promotions, and some of the most appealing offers—from top-rated cruise lines to flight fares—are already live. I've rounded up nine of the best early Travel Tuesday deals worth booking, or at the very least keeping an eye on as more are announced.

World of Hyatt has already dropped its annual Cyber Sale, slashing rates by up to 25% for its members across more than 1,250 hotels and luxury resorts across the globe. With a travel window stretching all the way through April 30, 2027, you have plenty of runway to lock in trips from a sun-drenched winter escape to a spring break getaway—or that bucket-list vacation you’ve been putting off. If you’re not a member yet, the sale is open to the general public for up to 20% off. (That said, signing up takes two seconds and is totally free, so don’t leave the money on the table!) Just make sure to lock in your dates by December 8, 2026.

Save on Sandals Saint Vincent and The Grenadines—the perfect sanctuary for relaxation within over 50 acres of breathtaking Jurassic Park–like scenery.

Select bookings promise some exclusive perks too: At Sandals Resorts specifically, travelers can receive up to $2,250 on booking and spa credits to use during their adults-only stay. Families booking Beaches Turks and Caicos (including the new Treasure Beach Village) or Beaches Negril in Jamaica can receive up to $1,650 in booking and spa credits. Just book by Travel Tuesday itself for qualifying travel through December 31, 2028.

Whether you’re an avid traveler or not, there’s a high chance you’ve booked a flight, hotel, or rental on Expedia. Lucky for you, now just so happens to be the site’s biggest sale of the year, with savings on family beach resorts, romantic getaways, cabin retreats, and everywhere in between. If you’ve already got a special destination in mind, simply enter your city of choice and travel dates into the website or app’s search bar, use filters to refine your search, and see which Travel Tuesday deals come rolling in. Up until December 3, those ready to book via Expedia can save up to 50% on stays in cities all over the world—plus, onboard perks on select cruises, eligible discounts on car rentals, and more.

In true holiday spirit, the ever-luxe and tropical hotel group Sun Siyam is offering up to 50% in savings across its six stunning resorts, from secluded barefoot hideaways in the Maldives to lush, high-end retreats in Sri Lanka. For those dreaming of the ends of the Earth, the cruise line is offering savings of up to 40% on select Arctic and Antarctic voyages. Available to book now through December 3, the limited-time promotion brings the world’s most exclusive polar frontiers within closer reach—from the icy wilderness of the Antarctic Peninsula and Svalbard to the rugged landscapes of Patagonia, Greenland, Iceland, and beyond. #6199. Delta Air Lines New-Hire Pilot Reportedly Fired After Answering His Cellphone While Taxiing

A new-hire Delta Air Lines pilot reportedly answered his cellphone while taxiing for departure, prompting the captain to return to the gate and have him removed. According to an account shared on the Black Box Aviation Podcast, the first officer subsequently lost his job. If accurate, this was a remarkably poor way to begin an airline career at Delta!

The story comes from the Black Box Aviation Podcast, which recently discussed distractions on the flight deck and the consequences of using personal phones while working.

According to the account, a Delta first officer was undergoing Initial Operating Experience, or IOE, when he answered his cellphone while the aircraft was taxiing for departure. Rather than continue to the runway, the captain returned to the gate. The first officer was removed and reportedly fired.

IOE involves flying actual airline trips under the supervision of a check pilot. A new hire may have substantial flying experience elsewhere, but is still learning how to apply the new airline’s procedures in everyday operations.

New-hire FO. First trip on the line. Taxiing out in Atlanta… and his phone rings. 📵Silence it? Nope. He ANSWERED it. 🤦‍♂️Captain went back to the gate, and that was the end of his dream job.🎧 Watch the full episode in the comments 👇#PilotLife #AirlinePilot #AvGeek pic.twitter.com/QefwSoTBiN

— The Blackbox Podcast (@the_black_box01) November 17, 2026

There are limitations to this account. I have not obtained confirmation from Delta (understandably, no response). Furthermore, no flight number or date was referenced, so the recent discussion does not necessarily imply that this just happened. The reported dismissal should be understood as the podcast’s account…and incidents like this have been part of airline pilot lore in online forums for many years.

I suspect some passengers might hear this story and think firing someone over a phone call sounds excessive. After all, the airplane was still on the ground.

But taxiing requires the attention of both pilots. A captain may be steering, but the first officer still has work to do, including monitoring the aircraft’s progress and air traffic control instructions. A wrong turn or missed runway instruction can have very serious consequences…being a pilot is one of the professions that leaves no room for error.

The federal sterile cockpit rule specifically includes taxi among the critical phases of flight. It prohibits activities that could distract flight crew members from their duties.

A separate provision restricts the use of personal wireless communications devices at a flight crew duty station during flight, with exceptions for specified purposes under approved airline procedures. The FAA’s guidance makes clear that prohibited personal use includes telephone conversations, texting, and browsing the internet.

Pilots can use approved electronic flight bags (EFBs are the iPads that replace paper manuals and charts) and make necessary operational communications. Taking an ordinary personal call while taxiing is another matter.

I spend far too much time on my phone, as my weekly screen time reports reminds me every Sunday morning. I understand how reflexively we reach for it when it rings or lights up. But there are times when it simply needs to remain put away, and working in the cockpit of a moving passenger jet is certainly one of them.

What strikes me about this account is the setting. This was reportedly a new hire being supervised during training. That should be a time to demonstrate that you understand the procedures and can be trusted to follow them!

If the account is complete and the call was personal, I understand why the captain would have concerns about continuing the flight with that first officer. Returning to the gate would inconvenience passengers, but I would rather be delayed than have a captain continue after losing confidence in the person beside him.

The employment decision is harder to assess without the full record. We do not know whether there were previous concerns or what explanation the first officer offered. I tend to be more forgiving and don’t think that every mistake during training should end a career. Even so, this would be a serious lapse in judgment. A pilot arriving at Delta should already understand why answering a personal call during taxi is unacceptable.

The Black Box Aviation Podcast recounts a Delta new-hire first officer answering his cellphone during taxi, being removed after a return to the gate, and subsequently losing his job. The incident remains unconfirmed beyond that account.

If it happened as described, I understand the captain’s decision. Passengers should be able to expect both pilots to give their attention to operating the aircraft safely. Answering personal phone call is unacceptable.

#6198. Where Was 'The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' Filmed? Behind the Scenes in Spain and Germany

On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television shows, and more. This time, we take a look at The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.

We’re heading back to Panem for the sixth time this autumn, as the latest Hunger Games prequel hits screens. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is set 24 years before the action of the first film and tells the origin story of Katniss Everdeen’s grumpy tutor, Haymitch Abernathy, as he enters the Games himself.

Joseph Zada as Haymitch Abernathy and Whitney Peak as Lenore Dove Baird

Based on the books by Suzanne Collins, the dystopian series is set in a futuristic America in which each district must send a teenage tribute to fight to the death in an annual competition—the idea being that, by doing so, the public will be too afraid to rebel against President Snow.

This edition of the games is known as the Quarter Quell, with double the number of tributes being sent into the arena, meaning the stakes are so much higher. Interest in the film is high, not least because Haymitch is so beloved in the original series, portrayed by Woody Harrelson. Newcomer Joseph Zada takes the lead role in the latest film, while Hollywood heavyweights Ralph Fiennes, Glenn Close, Elle Fanning, and Kieran Culkin also star.

One of the most important sets in the film is the arena where the games take place, and for this, director Francis Lawrence opted not for CGI and a green screen, but instead a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve in northern Spain. Below, we look into the locations used in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.

Ben Wang as Wyatt Callow, Percy Daggs IV as Ampert Latier, Joseph Zada as Haymitch Abernathy, and Mckenna Grace as Maysilee Donner in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping

Within the book and film series, the settings for the Hunger Games are always known to be virtually spectacular. For this film, filmmakers settled on the vast and untouched landscape of Somiedo Natural Park in the Asturias region of northern Spain, which boasts mountain ranges, glacial valleys, beautiful meadows, dense forests, and tranquil lakes. The remote region is also home to the last brown bear population in Europe.

When the tributes are launched into the arena, they are presented with a vast Cornucopia, a pile of weapons, food, and other supplies that might be useful to them in the competition. These scenes were filmed at Somiedo Natural Park, with the Asturian mountains and a glacial lake in the background.

“Somiedo is a spectacular place,” said Pedro Aráez, supervising location manager. “The valleys, forests, and mountains have a very wild, untouched feeling, which was exactly what the filmmakers were looking for. It’s remote, dramatic, and visually unique. When you arrive there, you immediately understand why it was chosen.”

Located close to Somiedo, the Teverga beech forest, Hayedo de Montegrande, was used for some of the dense woodland scenes, in which contestants battle it out and hide in the woods. Other scenes filmed here utilized a series of glacial lakes, the Saliencia Lakes and the Lago de la Cueva.

Iris Apatow as Proserpina Trinket and Elle Fanning as Effie Trinket in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping

Before the tributes are launched into the arena, they are first held in special little pods underground which are arranged in a circle around the Cornucopia. The perfect location for this? A velodrome, of course, which is steeply circular so cyclists can race around it. The film crew utilized Berlin’s Velodrom for this very purpose, with its cold, clinical silver decor perfect for matching the hi-tech aesthetic associated with the Capitol.

Prior to entering the Games, tributes must introduce themselves on the public stage, during a televised grand chariot parade in the Capitol. Another Berlin location with links to the sporting world was used for this purpose: the Olympiastadion. For fans of the earlier films, this is the moment when Jennifer Lawrence’s character Katniss becomes “the girl on fire” with her incredible flaming dress.

The futuristic architecture of Edificio Calatrava in Oviedo, Spain—with its striking, claw-like structure—stands in for a building in the Capitol, where President Snow and his government live. The complex was designed by Spanish architect Santiago Calatrava, whose work is known for resembling living organisms. Meanwhile, the 14th-century Ehreshoven Castle, just outside of Cologne, was also used as a filming location, with local press reporting that its lush interiors might have been used to stand in for somewhere inside the Capitol.

A former smelting factory complex in western Germany, Landschaftspark Duisburg-Nord provides the backdrop for one of the most atmospheric settings in the films, Haymitch’s home of District 12. The vast complex is able to stand in for multiple places within the district, a former mining town that has fallen on seriously bad times. Rather than being a desolate area stumbled upon by the filmmakers, Landschaftspark is popular for its nightly light installation by British artist Jonathan Park. There are also regular al fresco events here, from film screenings to the annual art-meets-sport Ruhr Games and Traumzeit Festival. Another location in Germany, Lindlar Quarry, was used for District 12, with wooden huts built here to resemble the outskirts of the village.

#6196. American Plans Return to Israel, Partners With Israir

After a three-year hiatus, American Airlines is preparing to resume service to Israel.

The carrier said Friday that it will restart flights from New York-JFK to Tel Aviv on March 27, 2027. Flights will operate daily using Boeing 777-200ER aircraft.

American has not flown to Israel since the Hamas attack on southern Israel in October 2023. It remained on the sidelines even as rivals United and Delta resumed service to Ben Gurion International Airport, though they too were forced to temporarily pause flights during fighting between Israel and Iran.

Israeli officials had questioned why American was slow to reconnect the country, citing the importance of air links between Tel Aviv and New York. The airline did not offer an explanation beyond concern for the safety of its passengers and crew.

American also said Friday that it has formed a commercial partnership with Tel Aviv-based low-cost carrier Israir. The agreement will expand in phases over time, American said; in the first phase, Israir will place its code on American’s flights between JFK and Tel Aviv.

The carriers will also work to implement an interline agreement that would give Israir customers access to American’s network across the U.S., Canada, Latin America, and the Caribbean from JFK.

“American looks forward to building a relationship with Israir that will give customers the convenient, well-connected travel options they desire,” American Senior Vice President of Alliances Anmol Bhargava said in a news release. “As we prepare to resume service between New York and Tel Aviv next spring, this partnership will help us deliver a stronger customer proposition in the market and create more opportunities for Israir’s travelers to connect beyond our JFK gateway.”

Israir operates five weekly flights between JFK and Tel Aviv using Airbus A330-200 aircraft. New York is its only U.S. destination; most of its network is concentrated in the Near East and Europe.

#6195. The Best Hotels Near Disneyland Paris With Cinderella Suites, 'Toy Story'–Themed Rooms, and Quaint Cottages

Located just 40 minutes from Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport, Disneyland Paris is the ideal place to begin a Parisian vacation or say au revoir before returning home. Disneyland Paris's two theme parks, Disneyland Park and Disney Adventure World, pair timeless charm with an ease you'll never find stateside. Here, you can sip Champagne in front of Sleeping Beauty's castle—or visit a dragon beneath it—while filling your days with delightful architecture, unprecedented thrills, and the wildest wilderness ride Disney's ever built (Big Thunder Mountain!).

There's also never been a better time to visit. Walt Disney Studios Park's March 2026 transformation into the new Disney Adventure World brought a drone-filled nighttime show, Avengers coaster, and even a Frozen-themed land featuring a lifelike Olaf robot to its once-faltering second gate. Now, between Fantasyland classics and futuristic favorites, there's something new and thrilling for the entire family to experience.

Of course, you'll need somewhere to rest your head at night, and that's where the best hotels near Disneyland Paris come into play. Staying at a Disney-branded property typically affords guests special amenities including ticket packages, exclusive character meet-and-greets, and Extra Magic Time, which provides bonus time in the parks prior to opening. These hotels are great options, but can also be pricey—luckily, there are also a few non-branded properties in the area that make for great alternatives. There's something here for everyone and every budget.

Unsure of whether you want to add something so Américain to your Paris vacation? As a theme park journalist who has visited all Disney parks worldwide, trust me: It's worth the visit. Even with so many cultural monuments in Paris, nothing is more delightfully uncanny than witnessing the United States section of It's a Small World. So, whether you're looking for glamour or simply a good location, read on for the very best hotels near Disneyland Paris.

Distance from Disneyland Paris: Three-minute walk

As the crown jewel of France's Disney resort, this 487-room property is Disney's best hotel overseas—and, quite possibly, in the entire world. After undergoing an extensive three-year overhaul, the iconic pink palace reopened in 2024 with princess suites and luxurious amenities worthy of its five-star ranking. Great for couples or families, guests can anticipate the ultimate royal treatment thanks to rooms with romantic castle views just steps from the park. With kids treatments at the Spa by Clarins and two complimentary hours of childcare each day, parents can unwind at the Fleur de Lys bar, enjoy a prix fixe meal at chef Jean Imbert's on-site restaurant, or perhaps even sneak back into the parks themselves. (We won't tell.)

Distance from Disneyland Paris: Eight-minute drive

Rustic-chic in the best of ways, Marriott's Village d'Île-de-France offers cozy abodes that sleep up to eight with full kitchens, washing machines, and plenty of space to stretch out, all a short shuttle ride from the theme parks. Designed to emulate the charms of a small Parisian village, these quaint studios and multi-bedroom town houses feel more like cottages than traditional vacation rentals. Surroundings like these may sound quotidien to someone like Princess Belle, but the resort is as sweet as the rooms are spacious, making it an ideal choice for a hotel near Disneyland Paris as well as extended trips to nearby towns.

Distance from Disneyland Paris: 10-minute walk, 10-minute drive

Considering it's the only hotel in the world dedicated to Marvel's famed comic book characters, it's no surprise the Infinity Stone–colored beverages and slick, silver rooms at Disney Hotel New York - The Art of Marvel are somewhat out of this world. Family-friendly amenities like superhero meet-and-greets and a design studio with character drawing experiences make it the ultimate getaway for any comic book–obsessed fan in your family. Yet, even with hundreds of unique pieces of artwork, it won't feel like you're living through an Infinity War. Delicately executed details, like Manhattan Restaurant's Asgard-inspired chandelier and Spider-Man swinging across the panel screens at Skyline Bar, provide simple city elegance with the lightest touch of Marvel magic.

Distance from Disneyland Paris: 17-minute walk, 8-minute drive

If this hotel reminds you of Walt Disney World's Yacht & Beach Club resorts, you're not mistaken—this 1,098-room Disneyland Paris hotel was inspired by its Florida counterpart. The nautical theming is strong, and it's that seaside charm that keeps parkgoers returning to this waterfront escape. Just a 15-minute walk from the park gates, guests can meet maritime Mickey & Minnie Mouse (who don delightful cruisewear) or indulge in a seafood buffet at the aptly named Cape Cod restaurant. It's modeled after a familiar location back in the States, sure, but after spending the day with princesses, dragons, and superheroes, you may find yourself overjoyed to return to those country club comforts.

Distance from Disneyland Paris: 13-minute walk, 8-minute drive

Craving a bit more theming on your Disneyland Paris trip? Look no further than this national park–inspired escape. It offers lodge-style living perfect for a wintertime trip. Cozy up to the Redwood Bar & Lounge hearth, or in one of the newly renovated rooms with nods to Bambi and Pocahontas, and take in the charms of what Disney does best. Multiple on-site buffets allow you to feast like you've been on the move all day because, well, you likely have.

Note that this Disney-operated hotel is currently undergoing a phased refurbishment. For stays in late 2026 and early 2027, I recommend selecting a refurbished room in The Lodges. Starting in February 2027, construction will move to general hotel spaces, and certain facilities will be temporarily unavailable.

Distance from Disneyland Paris: 30-minute walk, 10-minute drive

Rooms at the boutique Hôtel l’Elysée Val d’Europe are modern and minimal, offering the perfect escape from any theme park chaos. Though it's just a 30-minute walk or a short, free shuttle ride away from the gates, the real perk of being a bit removed is its proximity to the Val d’Europe shopping complex and the designer outlet mall La Vallée Village. With a bounty of discounted prices on luxury brands like Prada, Saint Laurent, and Gucci, you're sure to find a Parisian souvenir that'll rival the array of Mickey Mouse goods sold within the parks.

Distance from Disneyland Paris: Nine-minute drive

If the City of Lights appeals to you for its style and romance, consider this your ideal hotel. Design-forward rooms with concrete walls, sleek bathrooms, and an open, plant-walled lobby offer reliable value without sacrificing taste, making it a perfect choice for travelers seeking something a little less Disney. While families will benefit from select rooms offering full kitchens and stovetops, the upgraded amenities—which include a heated indoor pool, sauna, and hammam—offer a little something for everyone, just beyond the parks.

Distance from Disneyland Paris: 16-minute walk, 10-minute drive

Step right up to this quirky hotel that feels like a Western film set and is jam-packed with Toy Story details. Small touches, like cowprint bedspreads and appearances by Woody and Jessie, make Disney Hotel Cheyenne a hidden gem that's nearly as themed as Disneyland Paris's own Frontierland. Given that it's significantly more affordable than the majority of its Disneyland-owned counterparts yet retains perks like Extra Magic Time, this property offers a best-of-both-worlds approach for those who want to live a full Disney-fied day from first rides to fireworks.

Distance from Disneyland Paris: 10-minute drive

Multi-room cabins at this expansive, woodsy resort are the perfect way to experience a taste of the outdoors between trips on Big Thunder Mountain. Sadly, there are no theme park shuttle services, so parks must be reached by car, rideshare, or taxi. But that's not to say it's worth skipping—here, nature abounds in both form and function. There's an on-site aviary, comfort food at the Crockett's Tavern buffet, and plenty of rustic charm, so the comforts of home are never too far away. Consider this Disneyland Paris hotel as close as you can get to camping at Disneyland's theme parks—if camping also included unfettered access to Mickey waffles.

What area is the best to stay in when visiting Disneyland Paris?

Any hotel near Disney Village, the entertainment and dining district at the entrance to Disneyland Paris's two theme parks, is going to be the most convenient choice. This not only offers more ease and access, but affords you the option to shop and dine after the parks close each night. Still, booking nearly any Disney-operated hotel will give you benefits like Extra Magic Time and exclusive character encounters, which help get you even more out of your Disneyland Paris vacation.

Are there any hotels that are walking distance to Disneyland Paris?

Yes—but you might want to bring your sneakers. Disneyland Hotel is located directly at the entrance to Disneyland Paris, while Disney Hotel New York - The Art of Marvel, Disney Newport Bay Club, and Disney Sequoia Lodge are all a 10- to 15-minute walk through Disney Village to reach both parks. Disney Hotel Cheyenne is a further trek, about 15 to 20 minutes away, but absolutely doable. Shuttle buses are available as well.

What is the 3-2-1 rule at Disneyland Paris?

The 3-2-1 rule is essentially shorthand for how to streamline your Disneyland Paris experience. Experts recommend selecting three rides, two entertainment offerings, and one dining option for an easy, straightforward approach to planning a day at any Disney theme park. It works as well at Walt Disney World and Disneyland as it does here at Disneyland Paris, but I recommend you still do a little research before you go. Be sure you don't skip Phantom Manor, which can only be found in Paris, secure your dining reservations early, and don't miss the nighttime shows offered at both parks—they're among the best in the world.

It is best to stay within the park at Disneyland Paris, or outside of it?

It goes without saying that the closer you are to the castle, the “better” your hotel will be, but it shouldn't be a deal-breaker. Convenience is always a factor, but Disney-operated hotels at Disneyland Paris tend to be much pricier than their American counterparts, so staying a bus ride away might be necessary. Still, the perks are plenty across most of Disneyland's own hotels, including extra time in the parks, which is why I recommended so many of them.

#6194. Gabe Evans announces 2028 comeback bid from Boebert’s district

Rep. Gabe Evans, here arriving at the Capitol in July for a House Republican Conference meeting, lost his bid for a second term representing Colorado's 8th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Colorado Rep. Gabe Evans, who lost reelection earlier this month, announced Monday a 2028 run from the neighboring district of fellow defeated Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert.

“Now more than ever, Colorado needs conservatives in Congress who will fight to keep our border secure, cut taxes for working families, keep boys from dominating girls' sports and locker rooms, protect our water, and make energy affordable,” Evans said in a statement.

His announcement comes less than two weeks after he lost his bid for a second term representing the battleground 8th District in the Denver area. While the race had been considered one of the most competitive in the country, Democratic former state Rep. Manny Rutinel secured victory by 15 points.

As part of House Democrats’ massive midterm gains, they flipped three seats in Colorado. Boebert narrowly lost her reelection bid in the 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, while Republican Rep. Jeff Crank lost in the 5th District.

Evans’ statement cited his ties to the 4th District, which encompasses the eastern part of the state and extends into the Denver metro area.

“From Loveland to Lamar, I’m ready to keep fighting in the 4th District, where I grew up, and where my family has lived since 1976,” he said.

The district has a deep history of voting Republican. Boebert won by 11 points in 2024 while Donald Trump carried the district by 18 points.

Evans is far from the first member of Congress to switch to a district seen as more favorable to his party. Boebert herself shifted from Colorado's more competitive 3rd District to run for the heavily conservative 4th in 2024.

The 4th District will likely be a top target for Republicans in 2028, and Evans’ campaign sought to portray him as a clear front-runner in what could become a crowded GOP primary.

“Gabe Evans will enter 2027 and the race for Colorado’s 4th Congressional District with $300,000 in campaign funds and name recognition that no first-time candidate in the district could match,” his campaign said in the statement. “Combined with his record as an Army aviator, police officer, rancher, and member of Congress, that gives him a head start in money, name recognition, and credibility before the field takes shape.”

A former state legislator and Denver-area police officer, Evans also served 12 years in the Army. He was first elected to the House in 2024, unseating Democrat Yadira Caraveo, and currently sits on the Energy and Commerce and Homeland Security committees.

Laubacher, a Navy veteran who will take office on Jan. 3, is the first Democrat elected to represent the 4th District since Betsy Markey won her lone term in 2008. In response to Evans’ announcement, Laubacher’s campaign said she would be “focused on making Washington deliver” for district residents.

“There’s real work to do: ending the war in Iran that Gabe Evans voted six times to continue, lowering the cost of groceries and fertilizer that his eight votes for the tariffs helped drive up, and protecting the rural hospitals across the 4th district he voted to gut,” Laubacher spokesperson Taylor Gillespie said in a statement.

#6193. A Guide to NYC’s Little Italy—and the Culinary Gems Hidden Among the Tourist Traps

Contrary to other tourist-focused neighborhoods in New York (looking at you, Times Square), Little Italy boasts an innate charm that resonates with visitors and locals alike. Sandwiched between SoHo and the Lower East Side, this jewel box area is home to long-standing, family-owned restaurants and authentic Italian bakeries, the majority of which have been neighborhood staples for decades. Yet despite its touristy atmosphere, a unique feeling of old school New York magic hangs in the air; beyond the personality-less stands and souvenir shops, framed family photos on restaurant walls and structural imperfections of tenement buildings speak to a bygone area of the city’s past, evoking a sense of nostalgia that so many neighborhoods lack. Pop down to Mulberry Street and see for yourself—though be sure you know which spots are actually legit (that’s where we come in).

A note on how we’re defining the area: Over the years, Little Italy’s boundaries have shrunk to focus on the touristic area of Mulberry Street and its immediate surroundings. While the southern and western boundaries of Canal Street and Lafayette Streets remain unchanged, the historic easterly Bowery boundary has arguably shifted to Elizabeth Street; similarly, the northerly boundary of Kenmare has also condensed down, according to many, to Broome Street. For the sake of this piece, we’re using the boundaries of Lafayette Street, Canal Street, Elizabeth Street, and Broome Street as a happy medium.

Located in the heart of Little Italy, Umberto’s Clam House is best known for its—you guessed it, all things clams. The restaurant quickly garnered attention shortly after opening in 1972, when mobster Joe "Crazy Joe" Gallo was shot in the restaurant’s dining room. Like its mafia-related history, the food at Umberto’s is as Italian-American as it gets. Baked clams and fried calamari are the appetizer list’s biggest show-stoppers, while superbly chilled clams on the half-shell pair exquisitely with equally cold (and generously sized) cocktails from the bar. Seafood-focused mains are the name of the game here, including the garlicky linguini and clam sauce and recently resurfaced scungilli with pasta served with piping hot red sauce.

Address: 132 Mulberry Street, New York, NY 10013

For Italian-American eats in a less stereotypically Little Italy ambiance, Il Cortile is the way to go. Contrary to the old school Italian vibes found in the majority of the neighborhood’s restaurants, Il Cortile’s atrium-style glass ceiling and plant-filled room feel more like dining al fresco in Trastevere than the heart of Mulberry Street. The family-owned restaurant’s neighborhood roots date back to 1975, with a solid focus on Northern Italian cuisine. The homemade cheese ravioli and wood-fired pizzas are always a safe bet, though for meat lovers, springing for the Fettuccine di Parma made with sweet sausage and wild mushrooms won’t disappoint—and be sure to save room for the pillowy soft tiramisu made with creamy mascarpone and imported Italian ladyfingers drenched in espresso.

Address: 125 Mulberry St, New York, NY 10013

Original Vincent’s, often called The Original Vincent’s Clam Bar, is home to one of the richest restaurant success stories in Little Italy. Founded in 1904 by Giuseppe and Carmela Siano, the business began as a sidewalk street cart serving up fresh seafood and jars of homemade red sauce, available in mild, medium, and hot. Today, the restaurant sits on the corner of Mott and Hester Streets, and is still known for its signature gravies, baked clams, and linguini-based pasta dishes (don’t skip the frutti di mare). As in its earliest days, Original Vincent’s still sells jars of their red sauce to-go, making replicating the restaurant’s pasta dishes at home a breeze—simply grab a bottle of Chianti, cue up your Louis Primo playlist and voila.

Paesano of Mulberry Street is home to one of the coziest interiors in Little Italy, offering a peaceful refuge from the neighborhood bustle. Rustic twig bunches and leafy plants strung with twinkle lights hang from the ceiling, while traditional Italian frescos and framed family photographs adorn the whitewashed brick walls. Originally opened in 1961, the restaurant remains owned by the same family and continues to be known for their Southern Italian recipes, including linguini with clam sauce, wood-fired pizzas, and savory chicken marsala drenched in sautéed mushrooms. Meat lovers, don’t skip the restaurant’s signature Veal A La Paesano, featuring a juicy and tender veal base layered with thin slices of prosciutto, steamed broccoli, and gooey mozzarella cheese finished with succulent brown gravy.

Address: 136 Mulberry St, New York, NY 10013

For serious pizza lovers, a trip to Lombardi’s is a no-brainer. Tucked on the corner of Mott and Spring, this neighborhood institution is credited as America’s first pizzeria, originally founded by Gennaro Lombardi in 1905. Lombardi quickly rose to fame for his large, heavily-topped pies, which he baked in an on-site, coal-and-gas oven. The result? Smoky crusts topped with perfectly balanced tomato sauce and gobs of whole milk mozzarella—along with sweet Italian sausage and various other accoutrements. The interior oozes with classic New York charm, featuring tables clad in red-and-white checkered cloths and framed family photographs strung along the red-hued walls. Head’s up, the spot is cash only, and while there’s an ATM on site, we recommend coming prepared to avoid the withdrawal fee.

Address: 30 Spring St, New York, NY 10012

Pasquale Jones-12_2. Brussels Sprout Pizza with Red Onion, Smoked Mozzarella & Lemon

In a sea of mediocre neighborhood wine lists, Pasqule Jones offers a breath of fresh air for Little Italy exploring wine lovers. Situated on the cusp of the neighborhood’s boundaries (and easily identifiable by its rainbow neon lights), this Italian-American pizzeria first opened its doors in 2016 and quickly became a staple for industry folks and visiting oenophiles alike. Beloved for its wood-fired New York style pizzas (don’t miss the signature clam pie) and thick, homemade pastas, the restaurant’s warm-yet-casual ambiance is ideal for posting up with a pie and a bottle—especially if you’re after great Burgundy, Champagne, or Italian reds. Expect classic picks from Pierre-Yves Colin-Morey, Domaine de l’Arlot, and Vietti, as well ample fun and fresh selections from Sandlands, Chacra, and Domaine Gramenon.

Address: 187 Mulberry St, New York, NY 10012

Address: 195 Grand St, New York, NY 10013

Although less famous than nearby Ferrara, Caffé Palermo features the innate Italian charm one looks for when wandering the neighborhood. Owned and operated by Baby John DeLutro (the self-proclaimed “Cannoli King”) since 1973, the establishment lives up to its owner’s moniker, offering flavored iterations—including pistachio and hazelnut made with sweet ricotta cream, the former of which is one of the joint’s standouts—in perfectly crisp shells. What Palermo does have over Ferrara is a solid amount of outdoor seating, ideal for posting up with a cappuccino and people watching on Mulberry.

Address: 148 Mulberry St, New York, NY 10013

If you’re looking for a wine break between pizza and pastries, this is just the ticket. Located on Little Italy's western limits (Centre Street between Broome and Grand), this French-inspired wine bar offers extensive by-the-glass options and shareable bites, including cheese and charcuterie boards to larger main courses, including beef tartare and lemon spaghetti. The comprehensive wine list, which features anywhere from 750 to 1,000+ references at all times, leans unsurprisingly French, though ample selections from Italy, Spain, and the USA are also available. Our suggestion? Post up with a bottle of Grower Champagne and relish in the perfectly executed Parisian bar à vin ambiance.

Address: 249 Centre St, New York, NY 10013

Address: 409 Broome St, New York, NY 10013

Technically located on the cusp of Little Italy’s historic boundaries (Kenmare and Broome Streets), La Esquina offers a flavor-packed reprieve from the classic red-sauce joints synonymous with the neighborhood. Situated in a former counter deli, this multi-level Mexican hotspot is best known for its casual taqueria (located in ‘The Corner Deli’ space) serving tacos, tortas, and ceviche. However, for those looking for something a bit stronger, head through the secret door and down the stairs to find the restaurant’s underground speakeasy. Lit by candle and adorned with Lucha Libre posters, the bar’s high-energy ambiance is prime for enjoying queso fundido and smoky Mexican street corn (elotes callejeros) washed down with expertly crafted agave-based cocktails.

Address: 114 Kenmare St, New York, NY 10012
